Bone conduction headphones are ideal for activities where it is vital to be able to hear your surroundings. Walmart currently has a restored pair for $95 (originally $135.95 and $179.99 newly introduced).

They won't win any audio awards, but it's better than any built-in TV speakers, and for $79, it'll improve your experience without breaking the bank.

If you want to take things up a notch, consider this 5.1 channel sound system. Not only does it include far more channels than a single soundbar, but you're also adding a dedicated subwoofer to the mix. A subwoofer will make those thuds, explosions, and low vibrations much more pronounced than on a soundbar alone. For $149.99 (originally $249.99), you can get the ULTIMEA 5.1 surround sound system, which comes with a soundbar—replicating left, right, and center channels—two rear speakers, and a subwoofer.

In a recent development, I love projectors and Roku. To me, a Roku projector just makes sense, especially at $119.99 (originally $389.99). It's easy to set up; you just need an outlet nearby and to dim or turn off the lights. If you have Bluetooth speakers, you can hook them up to create a more immersive sound.

TCL makes one of the best QLEDs for the money, and their technology keeps getting better. This TV supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, and if you're a gamer, you get a refresh rate of 240Hz that is automatically triggered with its Auto Game Mode feature.

It's a solid choice for gaming, especially at this price point.

The Aurora 16 has a slightly slower processor, a dimmer display with half the refresh rate, a smaller battery, and a weaker graphics card, but given its price, it's great for a gamer looking for a solid gaming laptop in the $1,000 range.

Tech Report: How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • It has been revealed that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

It has been revealed that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

It has been revealed that “When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was key to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

In a recent development, for Crawford, the big lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

“The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

Still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

“Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado noted. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford said, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

50 Years Later, Rocky's Best Line Is Still The Greatest Underdog Quote In Movie History

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when we use the phrase "cinematic classic," there are some pretty universal movies that are likely to flash through one's mind.
  • The reception to "Rocky" upon release was a surprise for everyone involved.
  • Beyond the accolades though, 50 years later, "Rocky" is still so much more than a boxing movie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when we use the phrase "cinematic classic," there are some pretty universal movies that are likely to flash through one's mind. "The Godfather." "The Shawshank Redemption." "Psycho." "The Wizard of Oz." But undoubtedly amongst those all-time great titles is also "Rocky," the underdog story for the ages that made Sylvester Stallone a star.

The reception to "Rocky" upon release was a surprise for everyone involved. Not only was it a huge commercial hit, but it also went on to win Best Picture at the Oscars, with John G. Avildsen also winning Best Director. Not bad for a movie written and starring a guy nobody had really heard of before 1976.

Beyond the accolades though, 50 years later, "Rocky" is still so much more than a boxing movie. It's a remarkably crafted rags to riches story with a stellar performance by Stallone. It contains one of the best fights ever and the greatest training montage of all time. It also paved the way for a long-running, shockingly enduring franchise that led to some other great movies, including "Creed," which earned Stallone a Best Supporting Actor Oscar nomination decades after he first put on the gloves as Rocky Balboa.

For all of the movie's memorable moments and for all of its quotable lines, one quote sums up its underdog premise better than any other.

"All I wanna do is go the distance. Nobody's ever gone the distance with Creed, and if I can go that distance, you see, and that bell rings and I'm still standin', I'm gonna know for the first time in my life, see, that I weren't just another bum from the neighborhood." – Rocky Balboa.

This quote really sums up the mission statement of the first "Rocky" movie in a nutshell. It's a true underdog story, right up until the end. It wasn't ever about him winning. This is a man who had nothing, felt like nothing, and was very unhappy with life as it existed. Given the opportunity, he made the very most of it and proved what he needed to prove to the world yes but, more importantly, to himself.

In a recent development, the ending of "Rocky" proves that he's not just another bum from the neighborhood. Win, lose, or draw, he went the distance with Apollo Creed, which made him a winner in a more meaningful way than winning any single boxing match. It's more about the journey than the destination. It's easy to be concerned about winning or achieving some goal that we believe might finally fix that hole deep inside of us but Rocky Balboa, with this quote, demonstrates a timeless understanding of what really matters.

Winning is great, but winning can take many forms. Rocky didn't defeat Creed but he won. He won a sense of purpose. He won a life he enjoyed. He won Adrian. He won in a far more meaningful way. This quote, once the movie's ending hits, rings loud and carries a lot of emotional weight.

"You're gonna eat lightnin' and you're gonna crap thunder!".

"You stop this fight, I'll kill ya'!".

Sources indicate that "My old man, he was never too smart. He notes to me, 'You weren't born with much of a brain, so you better start using your body.' So I become a fighter.".

In a recent development, "Forget about sports as a profession. Sports make ya grunt and smell. See, be a thinker, not a stinker.".

"I been coming here for six years, and for six years ya been sticking it to me, and I wanna know how come!".

It has been revealed that "Apollo Creed vs. the Italian Stallion. Sounds like a damn monster movie!".

#74474. 8 Movie Trilogies Where The Second Movie Is The Best, Ranked

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1699 w)

8 Movie Trilogies Where The Second Movie Is The Best, Ranked

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nailing a movie trilogy from start to finish is no easy feat.
  • Recent findings suggest that there are other movie trilogies that stumble out of the gate or sag a little in the middle before sticking the landing with a grand finale, like The Good, the Bad and the Ugly capping off Sergio Leone’s Dollars trilogy.
  • It has been revealed that most rare of all are the trilogies that hold up across all three installments while peaking right in the middle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nailing a movie trilogy from start to finish is no easy feat. In fact, there’s lots of evidence to suggest that it’s actually brutally difficult. Think of the drop-off in quality that took down The Matrix’s original trilogy, or either the Jurassic Park or Jurassic World trilogies. They all started as masterpieces and ended messily.

Recent findings suggest that there are other movie trilogies that stumble out of the gate or sag a little in the middle before sticking the landing with a grand finale, like The Good, the Bad and the Ugly capping off Sergio Leone’s Dollars trilogy. Consistency is key, and it’s far from guaranteed.

It has been revealed that most rare of all are the trilogies that hold up across all three installments while peaking right in the middle. Sequels usually carry the burden of bridging an origin story to an endgame, where the fireworks really happen, but sometimes, the trend can be broken. In the case of these classic trilogies, which all have three great entries, the best came in the middle.

They have to have a definitive trilogy element: while some of the included examples continued in some form, they didn't have a fourth part that immediately followed. So no Aliens here, despite its masterpiece status, and no Captain America: The Winter Soldier or Terminator 2: Judgment Day. All three were the best movies in their respective series, but you have to draw the line somewhere.

All three of George Miller’s original Mad Max movies are very different. The first is a gritty, low-budget revenge thriller that weaponized Australia’s dusty apocalypse-like landscape just as much as Mel Gibson’s charm as the iconic road warrior. Beyond Thunderdome is weirder, more theatrical, and arguably more philosophical, but the 1981 middle chapter of the Mad Max trilogy is where Miller’s vision truly clicked.

Mad Max 2: The Road Warrior is a masterpiece that lives on the back of its breathless action, which Miller would later resurrect perfectly for soft reboot Fury Road. The freedom from having to build any backstory allowed the director to get right into it, dropping Max right into the middle of a chaotic wasteland riddled with grotesque scavengers. It’s all so good that you barely notice that nobody talks for much of it.

Long before comic book movies became billion-dollar studio tentpoles, Wesley Snipes gave us his still-definitive take on Marvel's top vampire. 1998 stylish vampire hunter hit Blade was a great adaptation of the popular Marvel comics that kicked open the door for Guillermo del Toro to take things in a more extreme and very much bloodier direction in the sequel. Blade Trinity did have its moments of campy fun, and it's probably remembered as worse than it actually was, but it was not a shadow on the accomplished movie that came before it, and the set stories have rather overshadowed the actual achievements of the movie.

In a recent development, blade 2, though, was a stroke of genius. It didn't require a massively complex story, but is still a massive achievement in Gothic atmosphere building, visceral violence, and excellent martial arts choreography. Inevitably, Del Toro brought his brilliant eye for grotesque creature design to make the monsters Blade was hunting that little bit more terrifying. The sequel's stakes are raised because of Blade's forced alliance with the vampires to take down the mutated rivers, and it's just an incredibly cool movie still.

Sources indicate that the first X-Men movie was basically proof of concept that ensemble superhero movies could work on the big screen, even though the scale was kept relatively modest by a sensible budget. There was also a fair amount of exposition in order to establish the world that we saw through the eyes of young mutant Rogue.

In a recent development, by the time the third movie came out, it was rather overstuffed and leaned a little too much into cheesiness for some people's tastes, but in comparison to some of the X-Men movies that have followed it, it was basically a five-star triumph. X-2 - or to give it its full (and goofy) Sunday school name - X2: X-Men United - took the training wheels off. In fact, it blew them off and was met with widespread critical acclaim.

The story deepened the franchise's mutant rights allegory while expanding the scope of the action. It opens with an incredible sequence of Nightcrawler attacking the White House, and everything shines with a slightly higher level of confidence than the first film. The ending is great and sets up probably a better sequel than the last one delivered, and even now, X2 is still one of the best sequels in comic book movie history.

Some might say that the idea of classifying the Lord of the Rings trilogy as three separate movies is largely redundant because they form such a tight, continuous narrative. But even then, the second chapter of Peter Jackson's sprawling epic outstrips both the charm of The Fellowship of the Ring and the epic conclusion of The Return of the King.

All three are towering achievements in fantasy filmmaking, but The Two Towers edges things out with some seriously stunning action and a grand emotional core that even surpasses the first movie. The Two Towers had the unenviable task of juggling three separate storylines without the clean beginning of The Fellowship, all set up for a conclusion of Return of the King. It is your typical bridge narrative, but actually turns that structure into a strength, introducing Gollum in what is still incredibly impressive digital work and centering its incredible third act on the Battle of Helm's Deep, which has more grit and tension than the massive but slightly more hollow Pelennor Fields battle of the finale.

It isn't the most fun comic book movie or, indeed, popcorn blockbuster of all time, but Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight took the excellent foundation established in Batman Begins and built an absolute masterpiece on top of it.

The Dark Knight Rises is sometimes criticized for sloppiness and how it brought Bruce Wayne's arc to a close, and Batman Begins is a little slower, but The Dark Knight is rightly considered the benchmark for modern comic book cinema.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, to its detriment, it's occasionally a little too easy for The Dark Knight to be swallowed under the emotional story of Heath's Oscar-winning turn as the Joker and tragic early death. But as irresistible as that performance is, if you view it as only part of The Dark Knight, its many assets, it actually becomes even more impressive.

Nolan made the sequel more like a sprawling urban crime drama, like Heat or The Town, with an incredibly strong script, pretty much perfect pacing, and an escalation between Batman, Harvey Dent, and the Joker that still feels suffocating watching it back today.

For good reason, The Empire Strikes Back is usually held up as the standard for great movie trilogies. After George Lucas had already changed pop culture forever with 1977's Star Wars, and before he brought the original trilogy to a close with the crowd-pleasing conclusion of Return of the Jedi, his 1980 sequel instantly became the top spot of the franchise that has never surrendered since.

Unthinkably, some critics were actually annoyed at the unresolved cliffhanger ending, but The Empire Strikes Back is indisputably a masterclass in blockbuster storytelling. It split up the heroes, introduced Yoda to expand the mysticism of the Force, and boldly allowed the villains to win, injecting genuine stakes and depth to the space opera. And of course, it culminates in the most famous plot twist in movie history that has been parodied endlessly, but never lost its impact.

Recent findings suggest that sam Raimi's 2002 Spider-Man almost perfectly captured the colourful spirit of Stan Lee and Steve Ditko's comics. Even though it's widely lambasted, the messier Spider-Man 3, which was notoriously meddled with at the studio level, still had lots of Raimi's signature charm and deserves more than its reputation. Between them sits the greatest superhero movie of the pre-MCU era.

Remarkably, the sequel perfected the superhero formula before the genre even really got off the ground. Spider-Man 2 adds emotional maturity and a nimble balance of humor, heart, and spectacle that Spider-Man 3 slightly fudged. Rather than simply throwing a bigger threat at Peter Parker, Raimi focused on adding his personal conflict and the cost of being a superhero, stripping Peter of his powers as his everyday life falls apart, and a newly introduced villain emerged.

Alfred Molina's tragic, surprisingly sympathetic portrayal of Doctor Octopus is still incredible, and the legendary runaway train sequence is one of the best Spider-Man movie sequences of all time.

In a recent development, when you think about it, Francis Ford Coppola's The Godfather Part II cheated by turning itself into two separate movies that run concurrently and which could both be considered masterpieces. The 1972 original was already incredible and is widely considered one of the greatest movies of all time. The Godfather Part Three doesn't deserve the decades it's spent as the franchise's punchbag, especially with the superior Coda cut out there now.

Recent findings suggest that by 1974, The Godfather Part II achieved the impossible by surpassing a near-perfect original, winning six Academy Awards, including Best Picture. It was the first sequel to claim Hollywood's most prized accolade, and achieved it by, at the same time, audaciously balancing its dual narratives. By intercutting between Vito Corleone's rise as a young immigrant in New York and Michael Corleone's paranoid consolidation of power decades later, Coppola transformed his gangster saga into something we hadn't seen before.

Al Pacino's Michael was a completely different animal: where the first movie tracks his reluctant fall into family business, Part II reveals the full extent of the moral rot sitting at the top of his power hierarchy does to him. Add to that Robert De Niro's excellent performances as Vito, and you have genuine magic. The sequel delivers a richer, darker, and more devastating portrait of the corrupting influence of power than either of the other two films in the already excellent series.

5 best fresh movies to stream this weekend on Netflix, Prime Video, Paramount+, and more (November 21-22)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fall is in full swing now, and the best streaming services are making it easy to spend these chilly evenings inside on the couch catching up on our watchlists.
  • It has been revealed that for starters, Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster just landed on paid video-on-demand platforms, so you can finally watch this star-studded epic fantasy from the comfort of your own couch.
  • So without further ado, let's dive into all the best latest movies on streaming to watch this weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fall is in full swing now, and the best streaming services are making it easy to spend these chilly evenings inside on the couch catching up on our watchlists. A ton of latest movies got added this week, including several of this year's biggest blockbusters, and I'm here to shout out the marquee picks of the bunch so you can skip the scrolling and get to streaming.

It has been revealed that for starters, Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster just landed on paid video-on-demand platforms, so you can finally watch this star-studded epic fantasy from the comfort of your own couch. Over on Netflix, you'll find one of this year's biggest horror movies that's getting Oscar buzz. Prime Video just got the perfect football season watch, and Paramount+ has all the "bah humbug!" you could ask for with Bill Murray's iconic Christmas movie performance.

So without further ado, let's dive into all the best latest movies on streaming to watch this weekend.

According to recent reports, once you've seen one Christopher Nolan movie, you've seem 'em all, and "The Odyssey" hits all the beats you'd expect. If it were me, I'd save my $20 and wait for "The Odyssey" to come to streaming sometime early next year, but if your family is keen on watching Anne Hathaway act circles around Matt Damon and Tom Holland this holiday season, you can buy it now on the usual storefronts.

In Nolan's take on Homer’s legendary epic, Odysseus (Matt Damon) is just as tortured and lost on his perilous journey home from the Trojan War. Along the way, he and his steadfast soldiers stumble on a sheep-herding cyclops (and nobody makes any jokes), sail past wailing sirens in what's easily Damon's strongest scene in the movie, and run afoul of every beastie they can while trying to get home to his wife, Penelope (Hathaway), and son, Telemachus (Holland). The upcoming James Bond steals the show as the slimey ringleader of Penelope's suitors who shouts about getting "these beggars out of here.".

Buy "The Odyssey" on Amazon or Apple now.

According to recent reports, football season is heating up, and Prime Video just added a biopic about one of the sport’s most beloved figures that's all but guaranteed to be a popular family movie night pick this holiday season. Nicolas Cage stars as the legendary coach and commentator John Madden, tracing his rise from a Super Bowl-winning partnership with Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis (Christian Bale) to becoming the voice of football for millions of fans — and the namesake of the wildly popular Madden NFL video game series.

Recent findings suggest that directed by David O. Russell ("American Hustle"), it’s a star-studded look at the man who transformed how generations of fans enjoy football, though whether it's worth your precious streaming is debatable. It's sitting at a rancid 15% on Rotten Tomatoes from critics, though audiences were warmer to it (54% on the Popcornmeter). I think the negative reviews are a bit harsh, though it takes a while for "Madden" to find its stride.

Watch "Madden" on Prime Video now.

"Obsession," the supernatural horror hit starring breakout Inde Navarrette that doubles as a litmus test for crappy men based on who they think is the villain, is finally on Netflix. It racked up over $524 million at the box office, making it the highest-grossing movie Focus Features has ever released. "Obsession" deserves all that buzz too. It's a simple premise executed so well that it left me shaking in the theater. And I watch a lot of horror movies.

Navarrette puts on an iconic performance as Nikki, a young woman who suddenly finds herself more than a little obsessed with her friend, Bear (Michael Johnston), after he makes a wish on a charm called a "One Wish Willow." He doesn't expect the thing to actually work, and when it does (and in horrifying fashion), her unhinged behavior sends him scrambling to find a way to break the spell. I can't sing Navarrette praises enough — Nikki is terrifyingly unhinged, and her mood swings and outbursts might have come off as more cartoonish than chilling with a less-skilled actor. I'm excited to see how she tackles Rogue in the "X-Men" reboot.

Watch "Obsession" on Netflix now.

Recent findings suggest that the only "Insidious" movies I revisit regularly are the first two (which you can also find on Netflix!), but since it's a series my mom and I loved watching together, you can bet I'll be sat in the theater for every upcoming installment. Since the last couple have been real stinkers, I didn't expect to have as much fun watching "Insidious: Out of the Further" as I did. Directed by Jacob Chase ("Come Play"), the latest chapter ditches the ghost-hunting Lambert family for Gemma (Amelia Eve), a mother raising her daughter in her childhood home. The same home where a young Gemma watched her mother kill herself while supernatural forces wreaked havoc.

It has been revealed that after a chilling premonition, she learns she can enter the Further, the shadowy realm of lost souls that fan-favorite parapsychologist Elise (Lin Shaye) explained to us in the first movie. Drawn to Gemma's light, demons start turning our world into their own personal playground. Campy, creepy and blessedly light on jump scares, "Out of the Further" is a pleasant enough horror chiller that should please fans of the franchise. I know that dental cleaning sequence will haunt my nightmares for years to come.

Watch "Insidious: Out of the Further" on Netflix now.

Instead of seeing "Ebenezer" in theaters this weekend, your time would be better spent revisiting this Bill Murray classic on Paramount+, if you ask me. This is your father's Christmas Carol, and after the Muppets version, it's probably my favorite rendition too, reimagining the classic Dickens plot as a modern fable that still hits just as hard today. Murray plays the curmudgeonly old man at the center of it all, Frank Cross, a cynical TV executive so consumed by chasing ratings that he doesn't think twice about firing an employee days before Christmas.

He's compelled to reconsider that decision when, on Christmas Eve, as he preps a live broadcast of “A Christmas Carol,” the ghost of his old mentor pays him a visit. You know the drill: Frank gets dragged through his past, present and future as one spirit after another tries to convince him to change his mean ol' ways. If the usual holiday cheer in these kinds of movies makes your teeth rot, the writing's smart-aleck bite and Murray's sneering meanness make "Scrooged" a nice palette cleanser.

Watch "Scrooged" on Paramount+ now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that effie Trinket, the character played by Elizabeth Banks in the original set of "Hunger Games" movies, is a larger-than-life, ridiculous, and flamboyant woman initially concerned with appearance above all else — even though her job is to beautify and briefly pamper impoverished children before they head to their deaths. It's hard to imagine this character, who appears in "The Hunger Games," "Catching Fire," and both parts of the adaptation of the book "Mockingjay," being played by anybody but Banks, yet the newest addition to the "Hunger Games" universe, the film version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," features a younger iteration of Effie. So, who brings her to life, and what role does Effie play in this prequel?

Suzanne Collins released the novel "Sunrise on the Reaping" in 2025, and before the book even hit shelves, a film adaptation (with the expanded title "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping") was in the works. Ultimately, Joseph Zada was cast as a young Haymitch Abernathy, the character made famous by Woody Harrelson alongside Banks in the first four "Hunger Games" movies. A ton of huge names, including Kieran Culkin, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, and Ralph Fiennes, went on to join the movie's cast from there, with Elle Fanning being recruited to fill Banks' sky-high pastel shoes and play Effie as well.

We see Effie in "Sunrise on the Reaping" as a fledgling stylist desperate to prove herself ... and not only does she end up styling Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes when a senior stylist falls through, but she provides emotional support to Haymitch before and after he wins the Games. But where have you seen Fanning before? Plenty of places.

Industry observers note that if the last name "Fanning" just looks familiar from the outset, that's because Elle Fanning and her older sister Dakota Fanning have been performing since they were kids. In fact, the younger Fanning played a younger version of her sister while making her film debut in "I Am Sam" in 2001.

Sources indicate that from there, Elle Fanning revealed up in family-friendly fare like "Daddy Day Care" and "Because of Winn-Dixie" (as well as considerably more adult films like "Babel"), but the fact of the matter is that Fanning essentially grew up on-screen. Both Fanning sisters navigated their journeys from child stars to adult actors in pretty incredible ways, but we're talking about Elle Fanning here, and her career does stand on its own. After playing younger roles in "Super 8," "We Bought a Zoo," and "Maleficent," she moved into more firmly adult parts in the films "The Neon Demon," "20th Century Women," "The Beguiled," and "Mary Shelley," just to name a few.

Without question, Fanning's most visible big-screen appearances aside from "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" have recently come in "A Complete Unknown," "Predator: Badlands," and "Sentimental Value." In "A Complete Unknown," she plays Sylvie Russo, the girlfriend to Timothée Chalamet's Bob Dylan and a character who's loosely based on Dylan's real girlfriend Suze Rotolo. In "Predator: Badlands," Fanning plays the protagonist Thia and her evil twin sister Tessa and was able to use her own odd physicality for the role. As for "Sentimental Value," Joachim Trier's gorgeous family drama earned Fanning her first Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress at the 2026 ceremony.

Industry observers note that remarkably, Elle Fanning's small-screen career is just as robust as her major-screen one — and she's earned almost as much acclaim to boot. I personally remember seeing the younger Fanning as early as 2006 in the particularly depraved "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" episode "Cage" (fans of that show know exactly which one I'm talking about), but 2020 marked her big TV break with "The Great," a truly great — pun intended! — historical drama that casts Fanning as Catherine the Great. In this deliberately anachronistic, deeply funny, and exceptionally bawdy series created by "The Favourite" screenwriter Tony McNamara, Fanning gets to play the future Empress of Russia alongside a deliciously clownish Nicholas Hoult as her power-hungry and utterly twisted husband Emperor Peter III ... and earned her first Emmy nomination for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series for her efforts.

Industry observers note that sadly, "The Great" ended in 2023 after only three seasons, although Fanning's next TV project, the crime drama miniseries "The Girl from Plainville," was well-received. In 2026, though, Fanning earned overwhelming acclaim and another Emmy nod for her lead role in "Margo's Got Money Troubles," a collaboration between A24 and Apple TV that proved to be one of the very best shows of the year. As a young single mother who launches an OnlyFans career as a colorful, coquettish alien to support her young son, Fanning is extraordinary as Margo, and it's clear that this ambitious and incredibly talented actor will keep racking up credits and accolades for years to come.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is right now in theaters.

'The Odyssey' Cast Debunks a Major Misconception About Working with Christopher Nolan

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that christopher Nolan doesn't exactly have a reputation for being the life of the party.
  • Sources indicate that but according to the cast and crew of The Odyssey, there's another side to Nolan that audiences might not expect.
  • Recent findings suggest that speaking with Polygon ahead of the film's home release, several members of the production shared what might surprise audiences about working with Nolan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that christopher Nolan doesn't exactly have a reputation for being the life of the party. The Oscar-winning director is known for meticulously constructed films, complicated narratives, and productions that demand an extraordinary amount of preparation. His movies routinely deal with weighty subjects, whether it's the nature of time, the consequences of scientific discovery, or humanity's place in the universe. Not exactly the kind of material that screams laugh riot.

Sources indicate that but according to the cast and crew of The Odyssey, there's another side to Nolan that audiences might not expect. Behind the intense focus and demanding production schedules is a filmmaker with a sharp sense of humor who genuinely loves being on a movie set.

Recent findings suggest that speaking with Polygon ahead of the film's home release, several members of the production shared what might surprise audiences about working with Nolan. Their answers revealed a director who enjoys a good joke, even if he isn't about to let it interfere with making a movie.

Himesh Patel, who plays Eurylochus, the second-in-command to Matt Damon's Odysseus, recalled a production that wasn't nearly as solemn as Nolan's reputation might suggest. According to Patel, Nolan's humor has a distinctly British quality.

"He's got a cutting sense of humor," Patel says. "It's that British sense of humor that can just be very sardonic. But I've always found it funny.".

That might surprise viewers who associate Nolan primarily with the intense atmosphere of films like Oppenheimer, Interstellar, and The Dark Knight. But Patel suggested that Nolan's enjoyment of filmmaking is just as evident as his attention to detail.

"There is a lot of fun because I think ultimately he takes the work seriously," Patel explains. "The bar is set very high. Everyone's there to work hard and fulfill the vision that we're there to fulfill. But he's also like a kid living his dreams.".

Patel suggested that Nolan is keenly aware of how fortunate he is to be making movies, and that enthusiasm extends to his willingness to get directly involved in the process.

Sources indicate that "That's why he likes to get his hands dirty. He likes to be a part of it, 'cause it's fun," Patel indicates. That doesn't mean the work is easy. Patel described a demanding production where the cast and crew could find themselves physically exhausted after a take. But those moments could also be surprisingly entertaining.

In a recent development, "The amount of times that we'd get a take and Matt [Damon] would be laughing and Chris would be finding it really funny, and we'd be sort of out of breath and exhausted," Patel recalls. "But it's part of the fun.".

Few people have a better understanding of Nolan's personality than Emma Thomas, his wife and longtime producing partner. Thomas has worked alongside Nolan throughout his filmmaking career, helping bring his ambitious projects to the screen. When asked what audiences might be surprised to learn about him, she pointed to his sense of humor.

"He's very funny. People always think that's a crazy thing," Thomas tells Polygon. "He's quite lighthearted on set.".

Thomas acknowledged that Nolan isn't always joking around. There are moments when the demands of directing require complete seriousness. She suggested that the place where he seems most comfortable is also the place where he's doing some of his most demanding work.

It has been revealed that "There's often times where he has to be dead serious to get the job done, but a movie set is his happy place," Thomas explains. "He is never happier than when he's standing on a movie set.".

It's an interesting contrast with the public image of a director whose work often explores serious subjects. For Thomas, though, Nolan's enjoyment of filmmaking is something she witnesses firsthand.

It has been revealed that matt Damon offered a slightly different perspective on Nolan's humor. Yes, the director enjoys a good joke, but there's a limit to how much time he's willing to spend laughing when there's a movie to make.

In a recent development, "I think people know how hard he pushes himself and everybody around him, in a good way," Damon tells Polygon. "But I think he's got a great sense of humor.".

Damon suggested that Nolan's reluctance to let the joking go too far has less to do with being overly serious and more to do with maintaining the production's momentum.

"He doesn't love to laugh because I think if you start laughing too much, it feels like you're not getting the work done," Damon explains. "But he does love a laugh.".

That distinction seems to capture Nolan's approach to directing. Humor is welcome, provided it doesn't bring the production to a standstill.

According to recent reports, "He won't let anyone get carried away," Damon notes. "The momentum is never gonna stop because he is a momentum-driven director.".

Recent findings suggest that special effects supervisor Scott Fisher described a similar atmosphere around the camera, where Nolan works closely with a relatively small group that includes cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema, visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson, and camera assistants. Fisher said there's often a little ribbing and joking among the group throughout the day.

"He's got a really good sense of humor, but he doesn't like to show too much," Fisher tells Polygon.

Jon Bernthal’s 6-Episode Noir Crime Thriller Deserved a Better Fate

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The classic noir detective comes with three staples: a gun, a smoking habit, and a three-piece suit.
  • Bernthal stars as LAPD Detective Joe Teague, who finds himself caught in the growing battle between Cohen’s criminal empire and the LAPD, with cops, gangsters, fixers, and other shady figures caught in the crossfire.
  • It has been revealed that mob City takes place in 1947 Los Angeles, where gangsters Mickey Cohen (Jeremy Luke), Ben “Bugsy” Siegel (Edward Burns), and Sid Rothman (Robert Knepper) rule the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The classic noir detective comes with three staples: a gun, a smoking habit, and a three-piece suit. While many actors have taken on the role, few embody it quite like Jon Bernthal in TNT’s Mob City. Based on John Buntin’s book L.A. Noir: The Struggle for the Soul of America’s Most Seductive City, the series captures the murky criminal underworld of 1947 Los Angeles, where a fictionalized version of notorious gangster Mickey Cohen rules the streets.

Bernthal stars as LAPD Detective Joe Teague, who finds himself caught in the growing battle between Cohen’s criminal empire and the LAPD, with cops, gangsters, fixers, and other shady figures caught in the crossfire. Although plenty of crime noirs have graced the screen, Mob City remains an underrated, short-lived gem that could have benefited from more seasons, with Bernthal doing what he does best: playing morally ambiguous characters.

It has been revealed that mob City takes place in 1947 Los Angeles, where gangsters Mickey Cohen (Jeremy Luke), Ben “Bugsy” Siegel (Edward Burns), and Sid Rothman (Robert Knepper) rule the city. Detective Joe is assigned to a special LAPD unit working to bring down the mafia once and for all. However, Joe has an agenda of his own, which begins to unfold when he crosses paths with Hecky Nash (Simon Pegg), a comedian with ties to Cohen.

In a recent development, one thing leads to another, and Joe finds himself committing a crime that could land him behind bars. He turns to his mafia-connected acquaintance, Ned Stax (Milo Ventimiglia), for help covering it up, but his actions don't go unnoticed by the mob. With both Cohen and LAPD Captain William Parker (Neal McDonough) watching his every move, Joe must walk a dangerous line between the two sides of one of the bloodiest gang wars to hit the streets of L.A.

Sources indicate that mob City has plenty going for it, starting with showrunner Frank Darabont behind the series. Like his previous project, The Walking Dead (which Bernthal also stars in), Mob City is just as invested in its characters as it is in its thriller elements. Joe isn't the only one guilty of being complicit, as neither the police nor the mob get an entirely clean image. With everyone having their own hidden agenda, audiences are left questioning whether there's such a thing as true righteousness in the City of Angels. Still, despite its heavy, philosophically nuanced tone, Mob City balances things out with the ensemble's sharp dialogue and the signature snappiness you'd expect from a noir series.

Sources indicate that visually, Mob City does a fantastic job recreating 1940s Los Angeles at its seediest. There's the hazy glamour the metropolis is notorious for, from smoky jazz bars and gambling dens to smaller details, like neon signs barely illuminating the streets. These touches give the series a cinematic quality that's rare for network TV. However, beneath all that glitz is a criminal underworld where violence can erupt without warning. Mobsters aren't afraid to pull out their guns and start shooting, whether they're in an empty park or a crowded restaurant. This contrast between LA's glamorous nightlife and its ever-present threat of violence makes Mob City such an atmospheric throwback to classic noir.

Mob City makes it clear what kind of detective Joe is from the beginning, describing him as a “gray man” in a world where good and bad are supposed to be as rigid as black and white. While most mob thrillers traditionally follow a “who's the mole?” plot, audiences already know there's a mole in the LAPD from the beginning — Joe himself. So, it's not a matter of finding out who the bad guy is. Instead, Mob City is more interested in exploring why Joe is so intent on breaking the rules and just how far he's willing to go to protect his dirty little secret.

In typical mafia stories, detectives in Joe's position are often motivated by monetary incentives in exchange for their cooperation. However, as Mob City progresses, audiences may be surprised to discover the real reason Joe is willing to compromise his badge and moral boundaries, which are well worth sticking around for. At just six episodes, Mob City is an easy binge compared to other detective thrillers. Unfortunately, TNT cancelled the show after its first season due to low viewership, leaving its cliffhanger ending unresolved. Considering its cast, production value, and potential to explore this fascinating yet very real chapter of L.A. history, Mob City deserved a much longer run.

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-announced third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest newly introduced director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

Sources indicate that “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really rapidly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” noted Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

It has been revealed that “It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” remarked Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” stated Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

Recent findings suggest that “People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” noted Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how rapidly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

Recent findings suggest that “I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” mentioned Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

Directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

Recent findings suggest that what Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly says he fell short in “Obsession.”.

“Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

Recent findings suggest that “Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” stated Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

Industry observers note that “I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

It has been revealed that “I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

Latest Update: Why Netflix's Fresh Dungeons & Dragons Series Is Dividing Fans

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, dungeons & Dragons is one of the most massive fantasy franchises in the world.
  • It has been revealed that however, translating Dungeons & Dragons to the screen has never been easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Memory Ngulube joined Screen Rant in April 2024 as part of the Movies and TV team. Since then, she has written for the Perennials and Streaming team, covering a wide range of topics from upcoming releases to old movies and TV shows. Memory is presently a Classic TV writer. Before joining Screen Rant, Memory was a freelance copywriter who specialized in email marketing and social media management. While she enjoyed her job, her true passion was always movies and TV. When she isn’t writing for Screen Rant, Memory can be found reading, baking (which is one of her passions), or watching her favorite K-drama.

According to recent reports, dungeons & Dragons is one of the most massive fantasy franchises in the world. Since its creation in the 1970s, the tabletop role-playing game has garnered a huge, growing fanbase spanning casual players, Dungeon Masters, fantasy enthusiasts, and gamers. D&D has deservedly become a cultural phenomenon that has influenced myriad media, from video games to blockbuster movies and television.

It has been revealed that however, translating Dungeons & Dragons to the screen has never been easy. Prime Video’s The Legend of Vox Machina and The Mighty Nein have given it a valiant effort and are easily the best TV shows inspired by D&D. Aside from the Prime Video series, the franchise has received multiple adaptations, including its animated series from the 1980s and the critically acclaimed Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves film in 2023.

Despite the success of some of these projects, D&D-inspired adaptations have often struggled to capture the magic that makes the game so beloved, leaving fans divided over how the franchise should be handled outside the tabletop experience. Now, Netflix is taking an ambitious step into the world of Dungeons & Dragons with Ravenloft, a live-action fantasy series centered on the origins of the infamous vampire Strahd von Zarovich.

Typically, books or games with a devoted fanbase face a lot of scrutiny when they are adapted for film or TV, and D&D is no different. While the franchise has been growing over the years and is no longer as niche as it used to be, there has never been a live-action series of Dungeons & Dragons. The Mighty Nein and Vox Machina have shown that the franchise works particularly well in animation, so it is a bit of a surprise that Netflix isn’t taking that route.

It has been revealed that ravenloft will not be leaning into traditional high fantasy, as fans would expect. Understandably, the D&D fanbase has been particularly vocal about Ravenloft because it isn't the kind of setting that seems likely to translate well on the small screen. It's an intriguing direction for a franchise with so many possibilities, but it also raises questions about whether Netflix is making the right creative choices. Previous D&D adaptations are exceptional because they lean into the franchise’s strength of great characters and intriguing adventures, so deviation from that is naturally going to raise eyebrows.

Netflix also has a notorious reputation for prematurely canceling TV demonstrates. The streaming giant has put so many of its original series on the chopping block that audiences are wary of investing time in a show that might not have longevity. There is a valid worry that if Ravenloft does not become an enormous success, then Netflix might cut its losses before the series properly builds its world or develops its characters.

With D&D fans notoriously passionate about the source material, the fresh series could become an exciting expansion of the franchise's mythology or another adaptation that struggles to meet the enormous expectations surrounding one of fantasy's most recognizable properties.

The concerns surrounding Netflix’s Ravenloft are valid, but that doesn't mean we should assume the series will be a flop simply because it uses a different storytelling approach than other D&D adaptations. Dungeons & Dragons has decades of lore, magical systems, and unique settings, and a live-action series allows Netflix to explore a different corner of that universe.

While not everyone is happy with Ravenloft as the show’s setting, it will give the franchise a chance to lean into gothic horror rather than fantasy alone. In fact, Ravenloft's isolated villages, imposing castles, and haunted forests are perfect for live-action. The upcoming Netflix series could appeal to people who’ve never heard of or even played D&D. Gothic horror, vampire mythology, tragic villains, and dark fantasy are all popular storytelling elements in their own right; the trick is just to ensure everything balances.

Recent findings suggest that the thing about popular franchises is that they can never please everyone. If Ravenloft were going to be an animated series, there would be a corner of the internet where fans would complain about having too many animated D&D TV highlights. In the case of Netflix’s live-action series, the discourse is that Ravenloft is too niche. However, the streaming giant has a real opportunity to do something truly special with the Ravenloft setting.

10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?).

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

Industry observers note that an isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

In a recent development, the Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

It has been revealed that is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Recent findings suggest that want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

Recent findings suggest that if you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous upcoming reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend notes a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

If you've ever struggled to keep a project organized or stay on top of a seemingly endless stream of emails, this could be one of the most useful ChatGPT upgrades yet.

Think of ChatGPT Space as a digital workspace that combines some of the best features of Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 and Notion with the intelligence of ChatGPT.

Rather than digging through old conversations to find something ChatGPT created, you can organize your work in one dedicated location.

In a recent development, at the heart of Space is a feature called Pages. These interactive documents can include text, images, charts, tables and even interactive tools. You can edit them yourself, ask ChatGPT to make changes or invite other people to collaborate.

You can also turn an existing ChatGPT conversation into a page without starting from scratch.

One of the biggest frustrations with using AI for productivity is that the information it generates can promptly become outdated.

ChatGPT Space aims to solve that problem with automated document updates. You can tell ChatGPT what information to revision, which connected apps to consult and how frequently to check them.

A weekly family planner that incorporates school announcements and upcoming appointments.

A daily to-do list that pulls action items from your emails.

A vacation itinerary that reflects new booking confirmations.

A job search tracker that incorporates responses from potential employers.

A project dashboard that reflects the latest conversations in Slack.

Instead of repeatedly asking ChatGPT for the same information, you can return to an existing document to review what's changed.

OpenAI is also bringing ChatGPT Slides to Space. Powered in part by Imagegen 2.6, the feature lets you create polished presentations, collaborate with others and ask ChatGPT to incorporate feedback.

Additionally, ChatGPT generates editable charts rather than static chart images. You can modify individual elements, export your presentation to PowerPoint and edit the underlying chart data in Excel.

For anyone who's ever spent an entire afternoon tweaking a PowerPoint presentation, this alone could make Space worth exploring.

You can start with a blank page, choose a template or turn an existing conversation into a document.

Industry observers note that try giving ChatGPT a prompt like this: Create a weekly personal dashboard with my upcoming commitments, outstanding tasks and important emails. Set it up to refresh every Monday morning using my connected apps.

You'll need to connect the relevant services and configure the recurring updates.

While much of the competition between ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude focuses on which AI model is smarter, Space now seems like a step toward making AI more useful in everyday life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Industry observers note that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he claims he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation A ‘Home Alone’ Legacyquel with Macaulay Culkin in Early Development with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg.

Industry observers note that but he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I remarked, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

According to recent reports, so instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

At the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he remarked. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

It has been revealed that his 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” remarked Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

How’s his French? “Zero,” he said. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” said Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

In a recent development, when it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” remarked Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

Recent findings suggest that one serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he noted. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

It has been revealed that of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

It has been revealed that the filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he stated. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

Was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he stated. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he mentioned, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.
