Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ankitg ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Vibecoding an inference chip

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ankitg

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that or rather, I vibe-coded an FPGA into running an LLM.
  • One of the more entertaining things about programming recently is that coding agents let me work in entirely new domains by giving me access to new programming languages and paradigms.
  • I overheard some founders recently talk about how FPGAs work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that or rather, I vibe-coded an FPGA into running an LLM. And it… just worked.

One of the more entertaining things about programming recently is that coding agents let me work in entirely new domains by giving me access to new programming languages and paradigms. Lately, that has meant hacking on hardware, now that writing low-level software is much easier. So, in this blog post, I’m going to try to recount the experience of vibe coding an FPGA, going through a series of “oh shit” moments several times, and giving myself a new appreciation for what’s possible if you have a large token budget (thanks YC) and interesting problems to point the models at.

I overheard some founders recently talk about how FPGAs work. I’ll admit I was relatively naive about them. I’d never really experimented with them in my startup or in college, so I knew little about them before. The basic idea I was familiar with: you can program a circuit into a reprogrammable chip. So rather than having a general purpose computing architecture (like a CPU) you can have a reprogrammable one, i.e. the configuration loaded onto the chip determines how its logic and routing are connected, and that (in theory) enables performance advantages. I also know that it took a mountain of C++ to write and involved manually analyzing waveforms for simulation and verification. I had never done this before though and it seemed cumbersome.

That’s about what I knew going into this.

According to recent reports, naturally, my ML brain thought “could we use these for AI inference”. I’m not the first to think this — there are a few repos attempting to port ML models to FPGAs on Github. But I hadn’t actually seen a writeup on whether coding agents are good at writing the low level C++ and Verilog code to program them and verifying the outputs so that they actually run accurately. (Spoiler alert, they are incredible at programming them.).

So I decided I needed to get my hands on one. AWS has F2 instances with FPGA hardware, and that seemed easier than going and buying physical hardware, so I asked Codex to spin up a reservation and got cooking. It had a relatively limited memory of 16 GB of FPGA HBM. Around the same time, I was working with the DeepGrove founders who were discussing their new ternary weight architecture that is well suited for memory limited cases. It’s SOTA on Mac hardware with actual agentic tool calling, so I figured why not, let’s see if I can get this working on an FPGA and fast enough to be useful.

What followed was a cloud agent running in Conductor for several days with me mostly just encouraging it periodically while it both (1) got a model fully running and (2) increased its speed by 33× from the first full-model bit-exact baseline to get it to a real-time relevant speed. It was one of the most mind blowing autoresearch loops I’ve run, ultimately writing roughly 3M lines across the experiment history and parsing 30M lines of output files, burning only $10,000 in Claude and OpenAI tokens to run hundreds of experiments. Most of the code is C++ and some Verilog. It’s been probably a decade since the last time I wrote any serious amount of C++ and I’ve never written Verilog. I honestly don’t know the first thing about Verilog. Most of my prompts were not particularly clever: they consisted mostly of me saying things like “you’re a superintelligent model, time to be more creative” and “let’s go for 2x faster, you got this”. Sometimes I brought some ML knowhow like “hey it’s time to consider speculative decoding” or “why is that running on CPU, you should port it”. But for the most part, it was just vibes and I’m pretty sure that with enough time the model would have figured out those things. Also, it seemed that both Astra and Opus (fresh Fable wasn’t out yet) were pretty capable at this and I could use them interchangeably. I’m sure someone has a good benchmark for which is smarter but both passed my smart-enough threshold.

Measured benchmark tokens/s · select a step to see what changed.

A head loader that reads both of its memory banks at once (+17.3%, measured on and off on one image), a runtime expert-prefetch policy, and the router-job timing fix; run one clock step lower (225/425 MHz) after a soak test found random faults at 231.25.

The chart follows the measured optimization sequence: 6 → 213 tokens/s, or 33× the baseline.

It has been revealed that at one point, around when it got to 10 TPS, I messaged the DeepGrove founders about this, and they replied surprised that it was working so easily, saying they had tried this a few months back and the models were not quite good enough to be particularly effective. They sent me a prompt that summarizes some of their lessons and I copy-pasted it into my session to see if it’d matter. It was essentially the most significant piece of actual guidance I added to this session. The prompt is reproduced below.

here is what someone else did for a dense bs=1 decode optimized fpga implementation for a dense qwen style model with ternary weights. you should take this with a grain of salt and pick things that you believe are acutally useful to add to your blueprint. Please also dont do things if you dont think is useful that take a lot of times like runnning really long test of a cycle accurate simulation etc or like physical design since those can take like hours. here are some ideas please pick and choose use this as context and not somehting that you shoudl be strictly guided by somethings that could help. prioritiize speed of like getting this up and running though..

The coding agent diligently considered these asks, but it didn’t seem to make all that much of a difference qualitatively. Indeed, when I asked it later to read all of the logs and determine which of these instructions it actually used, it said:.

Sources indicate that its biggest design ideas were already in my plan before you pasted it. You pasted it on Oct 29 at 21:50 UTC: 4,741 characters describing what someone else did for a dense, batch-1, ternary FPGA decoder. Within 70 seconds I had sorted it into ten ideas to adopt and five to reject, and written that into every design agent’s brief. The shorter remark from your friend Edward, about using lookup tables as logic gates, came 24 minutes earlier and left nothing on the speed line.

Design ideas I adopted: mostly confirmation.

Already planned: streaming weights straight into the compute lanes, running rows in parallel, and reading the attention cache in bursts were all in the design brief I’d released 35–40 minutes earlier.

Recent findings suggest that ideas I rejected: all five numerics shortcuts. Lower-precision activations, a deferred norm, an 8-bit KV cache, online softmax and 16-bit probabilities each change the output bits. That is where their design got its efficiency, and your bit-exact rule ruled it out.

Process advice: this changed things right away.

What you asked: not to do things that take hours.

What I stopped: a simulation that had run for about 24 hours, and two 250 MHz builds.

What I switched to: a short loop of C tests, synthesis and a logic-depth check, with one place-and-route per integration.

Likely gain: it got hardware results sooner.

Possible cost, which I can’t prove: two hangs that only RTL simulation could show reached the board the next day, and the massive integration lost 38 hours to them.

One real find it triggered. While checking their memory ideas, I found AWS’s own reference memory design, which reaches 426 GB/s across all 32 memory channels. The memory subsystem was built from it.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, for most of the actual design ideas it is unclear but there is good reason to believe the model would have figured them out, especially because it came up with them many cycles later after several compaction cycles. But the process advice was useful immediately for getting to hardware results sooner and increasing iteration speed. In other words, the humans are still useful at defining how to iterate fast and what correctness looks like, and the agents are great to manage the exploration.

In a recent development, here are the changes the autoresearch loop found. Interestingly, it’s mostly a series of modest improvements that compound 1.5x ish every time, rather than one or two giant ones.

Baseline: the first full-model bit-exact FPGA image (R8), served with host-side prefix caching.

Host software only: per-command overhead fell from ~10 ms to 0.9 ms (persistent register mapping, streaming reads, no per-command SDK calls or fsyncs).

1.25× this step · 1.25× from baseline.

A 128-lane attention engine that reads the KV cache in bursts instead of a word at a time, keeping the reference's exact summation order.

1.74× this step · 2.18× from baseline.

A parallel MoE router with an exact GCC-sort tie-breaker plus a streaming output head with built-in argmax; moderate-effort routing let it run at 250 MHz.

1.46× this step · 3.19× from baseline.

A glue engine that parallelizes norms, RoPE, quantization and copies between engines in certified exact orders.

1.47× this step · 4.70× from baseline.

The full new pipeline (streaming ternary projection lanes + a new sequencer replacing R8's control path), after fixing two hangs that only appeared in hardware.

1.63× this step · 7.65× from baseline.

Exact speculative decoding: the host drafts tokens by prompt lookup and the FPGA verifies several in one pass.

1.04× this step · 7.97× from baseline.

Fixed a relay that moved router weights between dies at 1/6 speed: router stall per layer 43,862 → 12,292 cycles.

1.14× this step · 9.08× from baseline.

Head shadow v2 (start the next token on a provisional guess; catch misses early) plus cross-die timing fixes, enabling 237.5 MHz kernel / 450 MHz memory.

1.62× this step · 14.68× from baseline.

Exact speculative decoding with a real draft model: a cut-down Maple on the F2's host CPUs drafts ahead, and the FPGA verifies every token.

1.12× this step · 16.42× from baseline.

Doubled the memory ports from 4 to 8 (two projection lanes, output head striped across banks): 1.39× per clock, but congestion cut the clock to 181/375 MHz.

1.03× this step · 16.91× from baseline.

Hid the attention engine's KV fetches behind its compute, and replaced the router's 2,048-step serial sum with an exact order-independent one (12,292 → 2,338 cycles per layer).

1.24× this step · 20.98× from baseline.

Lossless 5-trit weight packing (−20% weight bytes), shorter serial steps, and moving the output head to the far die, which relieved congestion and allowed 225/400 MHz.

1.27× this step · 26.63× from baseline.

Re-speculation after head-shadow misses, speculative MoE expert prefill during the router, and a die rebalance (without the unused DDR controller) that ran 231.25/450 MHz on both boots.

1.08× this step · 28.63× from baseline.

A head loader that reads both of its memory banks at once (+17.3%, measured on and off on one image), a runtime expert-prefetch policy, and the router-job timing fix; run one clock step lower (225/425 MHz) after a soak test found random faults at 231.25.

1.16× this step · 33.13× from baseline.

In a recent development, it’s difficult to do a 1:1 comparison across these configurations. I didn’t run the same autoresearch loop on every alternative, and I assume there is more performance to extract if I did. The point is to show how slow the FPGA was in its first implementation, and how far the optimization loop took it.

According to recent reports, the measurements below are from November 15 on AWS, replaying the same 8-chat × 3-turn benchmark. Prices are the on-demand rates recorded with that experiment. “Exact turns” counts outputs that matched the pinned CPU reference. The GPU implementations are included for context but did not satisfy the same bit-exact criterion but are pretty close in practice.

This is one generation starting with a 16-token prompt and continuing until the 8,192-token context is full: 8,176 generated tokens. The five middle columns show decode speed in tokens/s at the indicated context length for several generations of iteration. The last column is wall-clock time for the whole run/.

* For r8 and r9, the first two columns come from separate, shorter runs generating 2,032 tokens. The other columns come from the full-context run.

r9 improves short-context speed, while the complete long-context run is roughly tied with r8.

These examples come from the final r9 image.

246 tokens · 229.7 tokens/s · 1.16 s end to end.

140 tokens · 220.0 tokens/s · 0.76 s end to end.

System prompt: “You are a helpful assistant. Think briefly before you answer, then reply clearly and concisely.”.

According to recent reports, this was a fun project. I’m not sure I’m ever going to use this specific chip architecture in this specific way, and I’m certainly not claiming that an 8,192-token-context model running on an FPGA is the way I’d recommend anyone use something like this in production. But it’s pretty epic that this just works. Capability like this completely shifts the overton window for what a committed team of engineers can work on. It should mean that entirely new types of ideas (scientific discoveries, products, startups) are possible if you can point the models in the right direction. I’m excited to see what everyone builds.

#74432. Peter Jackson's The Lord Of The Rings Failed One Of Tolkien's Most Dangerous Villains

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (507 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Screenrant ↗ Open Full Page

Peter Jackson's The Lord Of The Rings Failed One Of Tolkien's Most Dangerous Villains

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings is an absolute masterpiece, a loving tribute to J.R.R.
  • Sources indicate that oddly, though, that's part of a wider mistake made in The Lord of the Rings.
  • Played by Brad Dourif, Grima Wormtongue was a manipulative adviser to King Théoden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings is an absolute masterpiece, a loving tribute to J.R.R. Tolkien's epic novels. They're not perfect, of course; despite their phenomenal length, they cut a huge number of scenes and plot elements. Tom Bombadil is missing, for example, while the final battle against Saruman at the Shire is completely absent. That particular cut has proven deeply controversial, with fans still debating it today.

Sources indicate that oddly, though, that's part of a wider mistake made in The Lord of the Rings. In the books, that Shire battle is the culmination of a story that played out very differently to Tolkien's movies. And, importantly, it means the Peter Jackson films actually failed one specific character—one of Tolkien's most complex villains.

Played by Brad Dourif, Grima Wormtongue was a manipulative adviser to King Théoden. In the books, he's a subtle schemer who'd been given his nickname by his political enemies, who'd learned to fear his Machiavellian cunning. Wormtongue was cruel and ambitious, a servant of Saruman who had proven far more successful than his master anticipated. He'd subtly undermined Théoden's reign, bringing the kingdom of Rohan to the brink of destruction.

Recent findings suggest that the book version of Grima Wormtongue doesn't achieve this through magic. Instead, he's simply the consumate politician, proof that you don't need physical power or sorcerous ability to be a dangerous villain. He reinforced this through the use of poisons, leaving his opponents under his thrall. He may have supposedly been an adviser, but the ambitious Grima Wormtongue had essentially taken over the entire kingdom before he was exposed and defeated by Gandalf the White.

Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings took a different approach, though. Here, the scene where Gandalf frees Théoden makes it abundantly clear he was enchanted; he has lost all strength and vitality because he is ensorcelled, unable to exercise free will. More to the point, when Gandalf breaks the spell, it isn't Wormtongue who is sent flying. No, Saruman himself is shocked as his power is broken, because he is the one who has really taken control of Rohan.

The difference is an important one. In Tolkien's books, Grima Wormtongue has a power all of his own, one not even Saruman possesses; he's still a tool, but one who is dangerous enough to operate independently, and who doesn't need the wizard's magic of Saruman to make him more dangerous. In contrast, in the films, he is essentially a channel; Saruman pours his magic through him, using Grime as a way to get to King Théoden. Wormtongue is, oddly, so much more dangerous.

Looking back, I can't help feeling Peter Jackson largely failed Grima Wormtongue. He turned Grima into something so much less than Tolkien intended, making him nothing more than a pawn (albeit one who eventually strikes back). Even his final scenes were rewritten, because Grima's compressed plotline was supposed to end at the Shire. It's one of the few missteps in Jackson's The Lord of the Rings.

If you're having trouble accessing certain Apple products and services today, you are not alone. As of early Tuesday afternoon, Downdetector highlights user reports of problems across multiple Apple services. While Apple's System Status page initially highlighted far fewer issues than Downdetector users reported, the site has since updated to reflect general outages.

According to Apple, the disruptions aren't quite as widespread: Apple indicates that the App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare on Devices, and Schoolwork are all experiencing outages. Apple says that the App Store and Apple Music "may be slow or unavailable," while AppleCare purchase is currently unavailable. The tech giant's System Status page demonstrates an "issue" with iCloud Account & Sign In. Other services with user reports on Downdetector, including the Apple Card, Apple Online Store, and Apple Business, read as "Available." Apple also says there was an outage with the Volume Purchase Program, but that has since been resolved.

Sources indicate that it's not clear what's causing the issues with the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud Account & Sign In, or other Apple services at this time. However, the timing is odd. It comes after a number of banks experienced outages on Monday, as well as Microsoft's massive outage the previous week. In addition to all of these outages, the FAA unexpectedly grounded all U.S. flights on Friday, for only the third time in the agency's history.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the day before Grand Theft Auto 6’s launch, like many gamers, I returned to Grand Theft Auto 5’s Los Santos for one last ride. Within moments of booting up my multi-hundred-hour save, I was causing chaos with a bazooka before switching to a devastating portable mini-gun. It was the stuff of pure GTA carnage; extreme violence, utterly gleeful in its sheer absurdity.

The next day, I spent the majority of my first hour with GTA 6, trying to decide what color to paint the protagonist’s bedroom walls, fixing the leaky roof, and replacing rotting wooden planks on a staircase, before unwinding by shooting some hoops in my front yard and going for a gentle kayak. I’d swapped being a one-man army for being a domesticated virtual boyfriend.

Sources indicate that I enjoyed my day of digital DIY significantly more than becoming the city’s most wanted. And that’s what makes GTA 6 a game-changer. It has literally changed the way I game. If previous Grand Theft Autos were sprawling sandboxes, ripe for wanton destruction, GTA 6’s Vice City is the first Rockstar Games world I don’t want to destroy; I just want to exist in.

Recent findings suggest that after 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived. Set in the state of Leonida, with Vice City at its heart, you play Jason and Lucia, two criminals forced into an increasingly dangerous situation as they seek their fortune, discovering the darker side of the sunniest spot in America.

According to recent reports, GTA 6 is still a Grand Theft Auto game, so the option to go on a rampage is very much present. If you want to play your Jason and/or Lucia as a murderous psychopath that robs every gas station they find, terrorizes ordinary citizens, and is hunted by the Vice City Police Department, Rockstar Games won’t stop you (though such criminal actions will be reflected in your “Criminal Profile,” which reportedly has narrative consequences).

According to recent reports, much to my surprise, I just haven’t felt the desire to engage in random acts of violence. Instead, I’ve been content to take my time, observing the world at a slower pace as a law-abiding citizen. I’ve even been obeying traffic laws!

But much to my surprise, as noted above, unlike in GTA 5, I just haven’t felt the desire to engage in random acts of violence. Instead, for the majority of my five hours with the game so far (a playtime that should swell significantly over the weekend), I’ve been content to take my time, observing the world at a slower pace as a law-abiding citizen. I’ve even been obeying traffic laws!

The DNA of Red Dead Redemption 2 has most definitely bled into GTA, and in my book, that’s a very good thing. Like that 2018 masterpiece, actions in GTA feel deliberate, and the level of detail in environments and how you can interact with the world is staggering. I can’t think of another AAA game that has made me want to work out, wolf down a protein bar, and take a shower afterwards. It’s not so much digital escapism as living a virtual second life.

Recent findings suggest that I’m typically a goal-oriented player; I like having something to do at all times. Which means with a lot of games, I find myself mission-hopping, neglecting to enjoy the setting in the process. With GTA 6, I’ve done the exact opposite. I’ve barely made any story progress, because I’ve been losing myself in Jason’s local neighborhood, pottering around shops, sitting by the beach drinking a smoothie, or taking to the ocean to see what sea life I can find.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The reason for my change in approach is probably that GTA 6 looks absolutely incredible on PS5 Pro. Yes, the 30 fps cap is disappointing, but the visual quality makes up for it. When an open-world setting looks this stunning and is rendered in such rich detail, perhaps it’s only natural to want to experience it as a real human would, rather than viewing it as a sandbox.

Sources indicate that maybe at some point, I’ll get bored of just existing in Leonaida (and I haven’t even been to Vice City yet), and then I’ll be glad to have the story missions to funnel me through over-the-top action set pieces. But at this early stage in my playthrough, the biggest joy that GTA 6 has brought me hasn’t been from stealing cars or robbing convenience stores, but just taking a lazy stroll.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

Sources indicate that “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang mentioned in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the firm, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

According to recent reports, even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s a familiar sight that could send a typical tech manager into hours of procrastination and avoidant behavior:.

It starts with a simple ask for a meeting or a presentation. No matter how pretty the template is, as soon as you decide you need “some slides,” you find yourself slinking down a path of obsessive pixel-pushing.

In a recent development, and it gets worse when inevitably you need a coworker to contribute some content. One understandably tries to cram as much text as possible into their space in 6pt font, while another (maybe a designer) prefers short sentences with bold words. You now get to make these look like they belong in the same presentation.

Five hours later, you have the perfect build, with diagrams and animations to make your slides more compelling, educational, and memorable. As you gaze upon your mediocre masterpiece, you wonder whether those hours were worth it.

You still need to communicate information with clarity, but maybe the medium has to change.

At Stripe, I have been accused of saying that we should ban slides. I may have mentioned these words in anger after the fourth meeting of the week where my slides’ colors were slightly wrong because someone had pasted them in and had “matched styles in this presentation.” Most of the time, this may be an eyesore but doesn’t really matter; in this case, my green “on track” status badge had morphed into a dull yellow in the new theme.

Recent findings suggest that I may not have meant it, but it’s an interesting provocation, especially when AI makes the alternatives much cheaper. Sometimes you have to take away the rotary phones to get people to use new technology.

So, I decided to try banning myself from creating slides for any reason, forcing myself to use AI to create interactive presentations instead.

Without much effort (and in under 30 minutes), you can create a Bauhaus-themed interactive strategy explainer….

Or a planetary system explaining what your team does….

This experiment has been surprisingly successful. Tired and busy Zoom brains might immediately check out when they see a slide deck, but a planetary system! Wow! That catches their attention long enough to get your point across, making meetings much more fun and efficient. And after the meeting, you can send them a link to explore the solar system on their own time. They may accidentally internalize your key points as they’re playing around with it. 🙂.

It has been revealed that with traditional slide decks, collaboration feels like a burden. Someone might mess up your template, or use the wrong font. At the end of the day, despite your efforts, slides made by different people who own just one section will likely result in a jarring experience (or at best a “mid” experience).

Sources indicate that on the other hand, everyone has fun building low-stakes, vibe-coded webpages together. I can ask my agent to fix the layout instead of moving everything around myself. I found that after folks see others doing it, they do it themselves because it saves time while allowing them to be more creative.

Moving towards the extreme end of collaboration, I created a village of cross-org tech leads as an icebreaker exercise for an onsite. I was nervous about how it’d go given how many humans and their agents were contributing, but folks seemed to enjoy vibe-adding themselves to our tech lead village, and an old, non-AI innovation called git kept everyone’s contributions manageable.

And they kept adding to it as the day progressed.

In a recent development, it started with a tech lead from Risk adding a dungeon and a dragon to represent the dragons the team slays for us. Inspired by that customization, others started to add their own. By the end of the day, there was a Live MaaS sign and the Pacifica Taco Bell representing the MaaS (Money as a Service) team. There was also a DEEP lake representing DEEP (Developer & End-user Experience Platform), filled with DEEP sea creatures.

Someone eventually added a way for tech leads to explore other teams, so we could see the inside of the Risk dungeon, the Pacifica Taco Bell, and the DEEP lake.

According to recent reports, this was the first time I’d seen people engage with the creation of an icebreaker activity or presentation beyond the bounds of the activity itself. Like, it’s literally fun to code with your coworkers and riff off of each other’s ideas. It’s all low-stakes code, and our agents help us write it and make small tweaks. If a different metaphor or idea comes to mind, you can ~easily and ~cheaply start from scratch.

Industry observers note that the village icebreaker got me rethinking other group activities I’d traditionally done in slides or Figma. Here’s a fun storybook holiday book exchange that I previously would have run in Figma, but is now interactive and ~infinitely customizable. If you’re at Stripe, you can just point your agent at the linked AGENTS.md and ask it to build one for your team on our internal infra.

This is basically just “how to vibe code a basic webpage with your friends,” but it’s worth writing down, as I find that folks sometimes hold themselves back from applying AI to well-understood use cases like creating compelling presentations.

I am impatient, so I prefer simplicity above all else. In fact, I find that simple prompts work best for divergent work like brainstorming, naming, or picking a visual direction. To that end, there’s nothing super fancy or really even a “workflow” to tell you about here. I asked my agent to put these steps together:.

Have an idea you want to present. This is the most vital part. Maybe it’s a doc, some quick bullets, or a stream of consciousness you sloppily typed on your phone on the ferry ride into the office.

According to recent reports, ask your coding agent for a few ways to explain it. Maybe it’s a lifecycle, a planetary system, or something you haven’t thought of. Have it make quick mocks so you can see what works. (You can repeat this step until you’re happy with the concept.).

Pick a concept and play with the visual style. I’m a fan of pixel art and Bauhaus, but you can ask your agent to cook up a few directions. Repeat until you find something you like.

Recent findings suggest that build it and iterate. Ask your agent to change the content, tweak the visuals, or add interactions and animations. You can get much more creative than you could in slides without moving every little thing yourself.

Make it easy for others to contribute. Ask your agent to create an AGENTS.md explaining how the project works and how to contribute. Then your coworkers and their agents can take it from there.

You can keep going forever, of course. I stop when I have something that gets the idea across. For me, this consistently takes less time than making slides, and my agent can crank away on iterations in the background.

Industry observers note that if you’re just presenting, you can run it locally; you only need to deploy it if you want others to explore on their own. And if you need presenter mode with your script, just ask your agent to build it.

It has been revealed that my pithy learning from this experiment: AI can help us create conditions for creativity to emerge, even when doing pre-singularity activities like presentation creation and icebreakers. When you make something people want to engage with, it unlocks more ideas, opens more doors, and hatches more dragons than a slide deck ever could.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as diametrically opposite to each other as they may sound, Warhammer and Studio Ghibli find common ground in a latest sci-fi series that arrived this month. What once was a niche British tabletop miniature wargame from Games Workshop has evolved into a multi-billion-dollar global entertainment behemoth rivaling sci-fi titans like Star Wars and Dune. Today, the grimdark 41st Millennium spans hundreds of bestselling Black Library novels and blockbuster video games like Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2, Rogue Trader, and Darktide, as well as Amazon Prime Video's acclaimed Secret Level episode, and a live-action cinematic universe at the moment in the works, spearheaded by Henry Cavill.

According to recent reports, on the opposite side of the spectrum, Studio Ghibli’s signature hand-drawn animation style is known for its gorgeous watercolor landscapes and atmospheric moments that allow quiet moments to steal the show. Ghibli movies prioritize organic movement, retro-futuristic flying machines, and famously, mouthwatering realistic feasts. Such a beautifully calm aesthetic has inspired a rich wave of non-Ghibli tributes across animation and other media, from acclaimed anime features like Mamoru Hosoda’s The Girl Who Leapt Through Time and Makoto Shinkai’s Children Who Chase Lost Voices to Western animated gems such as Song of the Sea and Luca, as well as video games like Spiritfarer and Baldo.

Warhammer 40K and Studio Ghibli couldn't be more different, but there's always a bold idea out there bringing two clashing concepts together.

Eisner-winning creator Daniel Warren Johnson returns to creator-owned sci-fi with Image Comics’ explosive new ongoing series Chainkata, which recently made its debut on November 18, 2026, and immediately sold out its 250,000-copy initial print run ahead of release. Developed over nine years since Johnson first sketched the protagonist in 2017, the forty-page premiere introduces Luma, the exiled warrior queen of a fallen kingdom who travels across deep space aboard her starship armed with a roaring chainsaw-sword. Although Luma longs for peace, bloodshed and interstellar terror pursue her through every black hole she crosses.

Recent findings suggest that chainkata shines brightest through Johnson’s fearless visual experimentation, with bold black-and-white ink work and brutal melee combat against painterly watercolor backdrops of swirling purple and blue nebulae, punctuated by sudden splashes of blood. This contrast captures the spirit of its famous pitch: "Princess Mononoke meets Warhammer 40K." Like Warhammer 40,000, the series revels in heavy-metal grimdark spectacle and visceral chainsword carnage, but it balances its furious action with the melancholic heart of a Studio Ghibli classic. Luma’s grief for her lost family and the quiet tragedy of her nature as a warrior forced to shed blood are patent in its art style.

In a recent development, chainkata creator Daniel Warren Johnson has built a signature style across several comic series. In Extremity, he delivered a post-apocalyptic revenge tale heavily inspired by Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind and Akira, mixing Hayao Miyazaki’s floating sky-islands and organic machinery with brutal war drama about the hollow cycle of vengeance. Johnson followed it with Murder Falcon, an exuberant heavy-metal adventure where a grieving guitarist summons a musclebound cyborg falcon through pure rock riffs to battle emotional monsters. Later, Do a Powerbomb! presents a necromantic tournament that infused professional wrestling with the heightened choreography of classic Dragon Ball fights and Japanese puroresu.

Sources indicate that daniel Warren Johnson brings the same synthesis of heart and spectacle to major licensed icons as well. In Marvel's Beta Ray Bill: Argent Star, Johnson sends Thor’s noble Korbinite ally on a cosmic quest to reclaim his warrior dignity. In DC's Wonder Woman: Dead Earth, he reimagined Diana Prince as a gauntleted wasteland survivor in a Mad Max-meets-Fist of the North Star apocalypse. More recently, his Eisner-winning run on Skybound’s Transformers revitalized the Autobots and Decepticons with its emotional rendition of the shapeshifting robots, while his poignant graphic novel The Moon is Following Us, co-created with Riley Rossmo, opted for a heartfelt take on bedtime-story magic.

Chainkata #1 is now available from Image Comics.

#74420. Breaking: 7 Classic Stephen King Books That Haven't Aged Perfectly

Breaking: 7 Classic Stephen King Books That Haven't Aged Perfectly

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The title of this whole article might look a bit incendiary, and sure, talking about these “aging badly” can be exhausting, especially when it’s not done with appropriate nuance.
  • Recent findings suggest that like, some of the Stephen King books that aren’t worth tackling are his newer ones without much that could be deemed problematic.
  • It’s not exactly niche in the overall scheme of things, but as far as Stephen King books go, The Talisman might qualify as a deep cut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Okay, don’t freak out too much. The title of this whole article might look a bit incendiary, and sure, talking about these “aging badly” can be exhausting, especially when it’s not done with appropriate nuance. But the person tackling this topic does love the work of Stephen King and wants to emphasize that while many of his older books have elements that date them, most are still pretty great. There are little things here and there that date them, honestly, rather than the bunch of them being outright broken when read today, versus how they might've been experienced some decades ago.

Recent findings suggest that like, some of the Stephen King books that aren’t worth tackling are his newer ones without much that could be deemed problematic. You should read all the books below before tackling the likes of Lisey’s Story, The Colorado Kid, and Cell, for some examples. And these books were all written more than 30 years ago, and some are closer to 50 years old. Times changing and things getting dated after that long? All that’s inevitable, and interesting to think about and address, all the while still stressing that these Stephen King books are still worth tackling, and that the smaller dated elements don’t really get in the way of appreciating the good stuff. See? Nuance! You're in good hands here, don’t worry.

It’s not exactly niche in the overall scheme of things, but as far as Stephen King books go, The Talisman might qualify as a deep cut. And it’s one where King was the co-author, since Peter Straub was also credited with writing The Talisman, and then its sequel, Black House. He was credited with Other Worlds Than These (2026), which concluded the trilogy, but that was more of a solo effort on King’s part, since Straub passed away in 2022.

It villainizes some types of people a bit casually, and then the character of Speedy Parker would be written differently nowadays.

Anyway, Black House and Other Worlds Than These have technically aged “better,” and they’ve also not aged as much objectively, but The Talisman is the strongest novel of the three. It villainizes some types of people a bit casually, and then the character of Speedy Parker would be written differently nowadays (and he kind of was, when he plays a smaller role in Other Worlds Than These), but 1984 was a while ago. You can find those smaller moments a little awkward, but they're not too extreme, and they’re also a very small part of what’s ultimately a very large – and sprawling – novel.

Industry observers note that it’s always tricky when a coming-of-age story tries to accurately portray the way kids talk. Like, once kids reach a certain age, they're potty-mouthed. You don’t always hear kids talking that way, because some avoid doing so around adults, but also, if you're an adult, obviously, you were once a kid. You were once one of those young people who refrained from swearing too much around parents and teachers, but let rip quite ridiculously around friends.

So, with The Body (a novella included in the collection Different Seasons), the kids swear a lot. That’s okay, even today, but maybe some of the slurs they use wouldn’t be included today, or if they were, the story would be more outwardly critical of such language. But you can argue it’s okay, in this instance, because these are boys who are rebelling (and doing something as daring as searching for a dead body), and further, the story’s set in the late 1950s, when things were less politically correct even compared to the early 1980s, when The Body was published. So, it’s a more minor example, but still worth noting for present purposes.

In a recent development, of all the books here, Christine might be the one that feels the least essential, or the least classic, but look, it was still written early on during Stephen King’s career, at a time when he was mostly putting out bangers, and Christine definitely has its fans. It being the weakest book of the first 10 or so years of his writing career isn't really all that bad a thing when it’s got so many classics it’s up against, and in the overall scheme of things, maybe it’s still a classic.

It’s got one of those typically gonzo high-concept Stephen King premises, since it’s about a possessed car that drives two friends apart. And some other things. Christine goes off in all sorts of strange directions, and all the while, you get some stuff that hasn’t really aged all that beautifully. But it’s the same sort of “problem” you get with The Body, because it’s about young characters who aren’t really supposed to be the most considerate of people, so it more or less works (it’s more the complications with quality, regarding Christine, that make it only sort of worthy of qualifying for inclusion in this particular ranking, with the word “Classic” being in the headline and all).

Industry observers note that there are only elements of Carrie that date it. That dating is okay when you consider the fact that it’s the oldest of King’s published novels, being his debut and all. And that sense of those small things being dated is further mitigated by the fact that the core of Carrie holds up and feels timeless, since it looks at bullying – both at school and a slightly different/more abusive sort at home – in an uncompromising way, and difficult experiences at home and school as a teenager? That’s always relevant, obviously.

It’s more the details in some smaller moments that are addressed either a bit fast or somewhat casually. There’s corporal punishment, some discomfort with Carrie casually wanting to act out violently before she actually snaps, and then even smaller things like smoking on school property. Like, yeah, you can tell it was written in the 1970s. It’s acceptable, though, and all the stuff that holds up and continues to be powerful is impressive. Some of those dated elements were why Mike Flanagan gave the world yet another Carrie adaptation in 2026; that one is decidedly more modern, and sure, intentionally doesn’t feel dated in the minor ways the original book (and the first adaptation, directed by Brian De Palma) might.

Like Carrie, Rage was a very early Stephen King book, being the first he wrote/published under his Richard Bachman pseudonym. And the books have another similarity, being set in high school and following a troubled individual who acts out in some kind of violent way, though Rage is a lot more realistic, and without supernatural elements, since that character’s a teenage boy who brings a gun to school and….

…Well, you do the math. He doesn’t go on a full-on rampage, but he commits some violence and then threatens to do more, which is where much of the tension and intentional discomfort of Rage comes in. This one’s undeniably controversial, though, since it was forward-thinking on one hand, being written before such violence in schools was as big a problem, but then a story about such a topic at all, and handled in this way, is uncomfortable in some potentially unintended ways. King himself seems to be of the opinion that Rage has aged poorly, since it’s the only Stephen King book that’s deliberately out of print (and therefore a little harder than usual to find a physical copy of).

The content is probably the biggest factor towards The Stand being a somewhat controversial Stephen King book, but then again, it is such a huge book (especially the uncut version from 1990). Also, this epic was written a while ago, so with more pages, there are going to be more opportunities for offense to be caused, and then with it being nearly half a century old, things might well be expected to feel dated.

It’s a book with a huge build-up to a conflict that involves the fate of what’s left of the world, and there’s also a lot of world-building, including some iffy stuff in terms of race and gender roles (to keep things vague, and not get bogged down in details). There’s also an extremity to some of the content of The Stand which is admittedly alarming, but at least some of it’s understandable. If you're looking at controversy more broadly, there is also the elephant in the room that is the ending to consider, but before then, and in terms of stuff that is technically dated, sure, you get a little of it throughout The Stand.

On the topic of absolutely incredible Stephen King books that are also incredibly long and quite controversial in parts, here’s IT, which has that infamous element involved in the ending, and it can’t be detailed here, but if you know, you know. As far as the basics of this one go, it’s hard to summarize the whole thing broadly, but essentially, IT is about a terrifying entity that takes on the form of all sorts of creatures and beings, including Pennywise the Clown.

It has been revealed that and that being terrorizes people in that unbelievably cursed town of Derry every 27 years, with the main characters fighting the titular villain as kids and then as adults 27 years later, with the timelines flipped between throughout the entirety of the novel. It’s thrilling stuff, but you do get a lot here that’s very eyebrow-raising, some of it intentional and some perhaps not so much (including that aspect of the ending, which is hard to overlook and even harder to describe while keeping things “safe for work,” so to speak).

Industry observers note that this repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it.

Sources indicate that the statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/. Each comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean, names the theorems whose statements must agree, and permits only the axioms propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice.

The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and time.

The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the paper indicates that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either.

The source of the paper is not in this repository.

It has been revealed that the package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes $(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$, one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled.

According to recent reports, VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the organization’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside upcoming features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the manufacturer’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the firm’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing users to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:.

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

It has been revealed that the first thing consumers will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the tech giant’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

Recent findings suggest that and speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for consumers looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow people to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Industry observers note that once customers are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, consumers can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

According to recent reports, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:.

'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (485 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • According to recent reports, as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's key to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

According to recent reports, as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that manufacturer or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

Next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Recent findings suggest that once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, revision the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

Industry News: Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

In a recent development, it's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Industry observers note that before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

According to recent reports, I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

It has been revealed that I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

In a recent development, I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

In a recent development, this BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

It has been revealed that the current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

How to stop weeds growing in your gravel: Experts reveal the foolproof method to halt the pesky growth

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I’m a huge fan of gravel and the small stones in my front and backyard — in fact, I’m even considering digging up most of my lawn next year to plant a dry garden — an approach that makes gravel even more central to the space.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is something charming about the crunch of gravel underfoot, and whether you are aiming for a relaxed rustic country look or strong architectural lines in a contemporary yard, gravel has a place in both.

I’m a huge fan of gravel and the small stones in my front and backyard — in fact, I’m even considering digging up most of my lawn next year to plant a dry garden — an approach that makes gravel even more central to the space.

Unfortunately, keeping gravel spotless can be a chore. Pesky weeds have a way of popping up and disturbing the landscaping. But it doesn’t have to be this way. With the right prep work and a few weed-removal tricks, if they do sprout up, you can enjoy the look without backbreaking weeding.

While gravel might seem far less hospitable to weeds than bare soil, they still manage to find a way. Wind, birds, and nearby plants constantly drop seeds between the stones, while fallen leaves and grass clippings gradually break down — creating just enough organic matter and moisture for those seeds to take root.

But weeds can also take root from below if the ground wasn’t prepared properly before the stones were laid.

The key to achieving a beautiful expanse of gravel, without a weed in sight, is to get the basics right.

Extensive ground prep ahead of time is really going to be the part that saves you the biggest headaches when putting down gravel.

Dawn DeFeo, head of landscaping & gardening at Landscape Barn, confirms, “Extensive ground prep ahead of time is really going to be the part that saves you the biggest headaches when putting down gravel.”.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Industry observers note that so what exactly does this involve? DeFeo says you need to start by removing any weeds and roots that are already there. And I know from experience that if you skip this step, you are already in trouble.

Once you’ve prepared the ground and removed any offending weeds, she recommends covering the base area with landscaping fabric, and adds, “Make sure you overlap a bit to stop new weeds from sneaking up through the seams.”.

Industry observers note that you might be wondering whether you need to lay down sand before placing the landscaping fabric, but DeFeo isn’t a fan. “A lot of people recommend it, but I’d skip the sand. It can actually work against you; weeds seem to like growing in it.”.

I have two different types of gravel in my yard: a large white stone covers a small space in my front yard, and I’ve laid finer pea gravel in my backyard. Both have fabric landscaping underneath that keeps most weeds at bay.

But what does DeFeo recommend? “Crushed gravel around a half inch does a good job fitting together as opposed to the smoother, rounder stuff,” notes DeFeo. “Just make sure to get a good three to four inches down so you can’t see any of your fabric.”.

Industry observers note that these garden gloves are made of nylon and nitrile and come in three sizes — small, medium and large. They offer excellent non-slip properties, are comfortable around the wrist, breathable and machine washable. At Tom's Guide, we recommend them as the best overall gardening glove.

Despite getting the groundwork right and laying a landscaping fabric and choosing stones that sit tightly together to stop seeds from penetrating, some weeds will still peek through.

Gillian Metetansky, founder of The Southern Garden Edit, explains why it’s not a foolproof method, “Weeds can still come via the wind blowing the seeds or through wildlife like birds spreading them.”.

There’s not much you can do to prevent nature from doing its thing, but by getting the groundwork right, it will be easier to keep on top of the weeds that do appear.

Weed patrolSo, what is the best method to remove weeds from gravel? “I only recommend removing weeds by using a vinegar spray and pulling them up from the base,” explains Metetansky.

Besides using the vinegar spray to remove weeds and pulling, she warns, “If you are not able to fully remove the base, they will come back more easily this way.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you are pulling weeds up by hand, De Foe recommends pulling them up after a good rain, when the ground is soft. It will make the task much easier, and it helps you grab the whole weed, including the root.

But what if this all sounds like hard work and you want an easier solution? "Using a weed killer isn’t the end of the world; just make sure to research the product, and keep in mind if you have kids or pets running around,” claims De Foe.

Sources indicate that avoid sharp toolsI own various weed-removal tools that I use to remove weeds from my lawn, pathways, and flowerbeds, and they are all fairly invasive. When it comes to gravel, though, I take extra care. The same sharp blade you might use to scrape weeds out of patio cracks can easily slice through the landscape fabric and encourage more weeds to break through.

Shift the debrisOne job that will prevent weeds from growing in your gravel is to keep the area tidy and remove any debris — especially in the fall when fallen leaves or pine needles build up quickly. “It will save you a lot of time down the road, and those leaves can become a new base for weeds to grow if left alone for an extended period of time,” she adds.

Google Wallet is now available on iOS to “organize purchases, tickets, boarding passes, and more in one easy place” in the US.

The Google Wallet app on iPhone does not offer tap-to-pay functionality due to platform restrictions. Instead, Google touts three intended use cases:.

App navigation is handled by a floating pill (in Liquid Glass) with two tabs. The homepage starts with a carousel of recent purchases slated for delivery, followed by boarding passes, and finally a grid of loyalty cards.

Sources indicate that the next tab demonstrates a list of recent transactions associated with Google. The Wallet app will display purchase emails and summarize them. You also get a list of Passes, which you can pin/unpin from the homepage, and payment methods saved to your Google Account.

The ‘plus’ FAB (floating action button) lets you add loyalty, gift, and payment cards (for use in Chrome). There’s a convenient “Everything else” camera scanner that can be used to digitize anything else.

The other main reason Google Wallet now exists on iOS is that the company wants the app to be a “secure hub for managing agentic purchases across Google.”.

Latest Update: DreamCoder: Coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs
