💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers.
  • Sources indicate that because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save major on a few worthy Kindle alternatives.
  • The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Sources indicate that because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save major on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the firm introduced a fresh model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

It has been revealed that if you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

Sources indicate that if you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is right now $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

Sources indicate that if you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, currently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.).

According to recent reports, if you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (right now $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

Sources indicate that in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#74291. How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.
  • Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S.
  • Sources indicate that in the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.

Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

Sources indicate that in the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

Industry observers note that at the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

Sources indicate that within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he indicates, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

What’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” notes Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”.

Industry observers note that at Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The company says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies.

This ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

In a recent development, among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

Recent findings suggest that to that end, the firm is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta indicates its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO.

Industry observers note that “We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” states Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The company is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby notes the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, New York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.Beta TechnologiesBecause individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation. Beta Technologies, Made in Vermont Beta TechnologiesAccording to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company currently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.

Beta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.

Recent findings suggest that “One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” notes Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.

Industry observers note that electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one substantial engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.

Sources indicate that there is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation.

According to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a substantial part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company right now employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.

As befits an aviation firm, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

Electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

According to recent reports, that helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

In Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

Kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the manufacturer’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies.

Recent findings suggest that by contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

“One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” claims Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them massive. This limitation is from the batteries.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

According to recent reports, beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

Industry observers note that the burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

On Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

According to recent reports, the modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the company is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

In a recent development, what sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

Sources indicate that for instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The organization has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

Beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The firm uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies.

Further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging intends is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the tech giant’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

The charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one important difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

For charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

Back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

According to recent reports, then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

Latest Update: I tested the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's weird rear screen — and it's actually useful

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I have many gripes with modern smartphones, but one of the things that really grinds my gears is the trend of Godzilla-sized camera bumps on the backs of phones, Apple's doing it, Samsung' seems to be planning on it, and a lot of Chinese brands look like they've been hit by a rogue hockey puck.
  • Xiaomi has taken on the task of making the most out of that normally-wasted space on the camera bump by turning it into a screen.
  • But the question is not whether the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's Back Display is interesting, it's whether it's able to justify its own existence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I have many gripes with modern smartphones, but one of the things that really grinds my gears is the trend of Godzilla-sized camera bumps on the backs of phones, Apple's doing it, Samsung' seems to be planning on it, and a lot of Chinese brands look like they've been hit by a rogue hockey puck. I've been testing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which also has a large, iPhone-looking camera bump, but this time things are different.

Xiaomi has taken on the task of making the most out of that normally-wasted space on the camera bump by turning it into a screen. This is not the first phone to feature a rear-mounted screen, or even the first Xiaomi flagship to do so, but in a world of phones that all seem to feel and look the same, it's quite exciting to see a phone organization offer something that helps its phones stand out.

But the question is not whether the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's Back Display is interesting, it's whether it's able to justify its own existence.

In a recent development, looking at the 18 Pro Max, my mind immediately jumped to the cover displays on compact foldables. The way the display wraps around the two main cameras is reminiscent of the Galaxy Z Flip 8 and the Motorola Razr. It's a little smaller than those screens, measuring 2.9-inches compared to those 4+-inch screens, but all three share a common purpose.

This is a way to use your phone without actually using your phone, using the smaller screen to look at basic information like the time or notifications on a smaller and more power-efficient display. At the same time, and as Xiaomi is keen to emphasize, it's a way to customize the look and feel of your phone in a way that cases and other accessories just can't manage.

Sources indicate that my initial thoughts upon looking at the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max and playing around with the screen weren't totally positive. I couldn't stop comparing it to the cover screens on foldable phones, and the fact that those screens are front-and-center when you take out your device. Xiaomi's screen is on the back, which is not part of my phone I tend to pay very much attention to.

But the more I used it, and the more I figured out that it wasn't just a glorified clock and notification alert, the more I realized that my initial reaction was the wrong way of looking at things.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The idea that this is potentially a very valuable feature clicked when I opened up the camera on the Back Display. This allows you to take selfies using the main cameras, in a similar fashion to foldable phones, using the rear-mounted screen as a viewfinder. This means you're taking selfies with the 200MP main camera, rather than the lower resolution hole-punch camera on the front.

It has been revealed that I'm not going to lie, though. This isn't a fully-fledged phone screen capable of running all the apps and services that you've got installed. It is significantly more limited than that, and the difference is like describing the difference between a smart home hub and a tablet.

The home hub may be useful for its own specific use case, but it doesn't have the same versatility or usefulness as a tablet running Android or iPadOS.

In a recent development, the Back Display is great for glancing at notifications and the time, especially if you tend to leave your phone lying face down. It even supports Live Activities on a handful of apps, including letting you control music playback on Spotify. Plus, it's possible to customize your screen with different backgrounds and clockfaces, depending on what your own personal tastes and style might be.

So far so good, though I can't say that I've ever felt using my main screen for those tasks has ever been a particular burden — especially since I'm just not used to looking at the back of my phone.

Then again, if you already have a smartwatch, that's not going to mean much, since you already have the bulk of this information available on your wrist.

Xiaomi does seem to be hinging on Generative AI to turn this screen from a gimmick into something you'll want to use throughout the day, thanks to a built-in system that lets you vibe code your own apps.

According to recent reports, anyone that remembers the flop that was Windows Phone will know that success of a mobile platform hinges on app support. Your apps give the system value, and without developers actively contributing to an app store, there's little reason for people to actually invest in one of your devices.

Sources indicate that so how do you get app developers on board to add utility to a niche display on the back of a handful of phones? You don't. You hand that job to the users, and let generative AI do all the hard work. So Xiaomi added a prompt-based system for creating Back Display apps from scratch, as well as an App Store of sorts that lets you see a curated selection of what other people have created.

Recent findings suggest that options I can see include workout schedules, mini games, educational tools, timers, and all kinds of different options, though I have no idea how effective or accurate they actually are compared to full-coded apps. Still, it's nice to see that there's a way to improve the usefulness of the Back Display — even if it would be nice to have proper Android apps on offer.

I found that basic prompts did work, but the more detail you could offer the better the outcome. Xiaomi can "polish" your prompt to better your chances of generating a usable app.

It has been revealed that however, this does not guarantee that the app would successfully generate — or that it would work. It took me multiple attempts to create a Doom clone, and even when it did, I kept getting killed off by a monster hiding out of my line of sight.

It has been revealed that so it's not quite as painless as having a developer-made app, and playing games on a small screen isn't ideal. But in the absence of additional features, this system is fairly good at filling that niche.

Industry observers note that I've spent my entire life looking at the front of my phone, and never really concerning myself with what's on the back. Even in the pre-smartphone era the screen was everything, whereas the back was just... not key. If rear screens start to take off, that could change the way people interact with their phones in a big way. And that's obviously going to take a lot of getting used to.

It has been revealed that that's probably the biggest hurdle these rear screens will face. There's certainly no shortage of utility, especially with the generative AI apps. It's just reprogramming user habits to glance at the back of the phone rather than looking at their main display. It's going to be an uphill battle to convince people that these screens are worth it, especially when they have to compete with wearables.

According to recent reports, if it weren't for the AI apps I'd say these screens don't have much of a chance. I'm not convinced that they will take off, aside from a few niche gimmicks, but at least they have some sort of unique selling point to work with.

Breaking: If You Loved 'Phony,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us.
  • Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).
  • Industry observers note that A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar shows) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

Industry observers note that A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

In a recent development, looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

Sources indicate that the Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a new employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that on one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

Apple releases HomeView 27.2.1 update, here’s what’s new

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that apple has just released its first post-launch software upgrade for the HomeView, version 27.2.1 which includes several bug fixes. Here’s how to install it.

Last week the Apple HomeView arrived in users’ homes and immediately required a software revision to version 27.2.

But now, Apple has already released its first post-launch update.

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, at the moment the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and consumers who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

In a recent development, the SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

Industry observers note that it comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple notes the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

Industry observers note that if your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

In a recent development, yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Industry observers note that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Legendary commentator CLIVE TYLDESLEY on how his ITV exit has made hearts grow fonder, the rise of YouTube streamers, his lockdown money-spinner - and why he refuses to be another loud voice in the game

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Clive Tyldesley reaches for his glasses as he rummages through the commentary charts crammed into an old filing cabinet, jokes about his fading eyesight and supposes one day he will no longer be able to identify footballers from the gantry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MATT BARLOW, FOOTBALL WRITER.

Published: 02:01 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 14:00 EST, 15 November 2026.

Clive Tyldesley reaches for his glasses as he rummages through the commentary charts crammed into an old filing cabinet, jokes about his fading eyesight and supposes one day he will no longer be able to identify footballers from the gantry.

Industry observers note that fortunately, we are still far from that point. At 72, Tyldesley is calling the game as accurately as ever. His eyes are perfectly good when bespectacled, his mind nimble enough to keep up with play and his soothingly familiar voice strong and authoritative with a gentle tendency towards self-deprecation.

This much was evident as Manchester United roared back to beat Roma in the Champions League and a clip of his spine-tingling commentary from the live CBS broadcast circulated on social media and found an appreciative audience in Europe.

'I don't know if there's an element of nostalgia in hearing my voice again,' says Tyldesley. 'If I'm honest, I've dodged the worst of the public's ire with everything including commentators because I haven't been around for the last few years.

'Absence has made a few hearts grow a little fonder towards me and maybe if I'd been on Sky every week for the last six years, I'd be no less unpopular than anybody else out there. So, I can't pretend it's not nice to get some engagement with an audience I used to commentate to on a regular basis, but I'm very happy where I am.'.

Tyldesley has been the lead commentator for the CBS coverage of the Champions League since 2020, converting transfer fees into US dollars and keeping his measurements imperial for a North American audience but otherwise approaching the job as he always did.

Clive Tyldesley is calling the game as accurately as ever at 72 and is 'very happy' in his role as the lead commentator of CBS coverage of the Champions League.

Tyldesley's commentary of Man United's comeback against Roma circulated on social media and received an appreciative audience in Europe.

The 72-year-old wonders whether there was an element of nostalgia to the reaction, with Tyldesley's work for CBS meaning his commentary cannot be shown in Europe.

Clips of the studio panel featuring Thierry Henry, Micah Richards, Jamie Carragher and presenter Kate Scott are popular on social media but live action featuring Tyldesley's commentary is governed by broadcasting rights deals and cannot be shown in Europe.

The one from Old Trafford of Matheus Cunha's winning goal in the 86th minute slipped through the net on X and reminded everyone his passion for football is undimmed, and his voice can still stand hairs on attention.

'I don't think I've seen a better game than the first leg of the Paris Saint-Germain v Bayern Munich Champions League semi-final,' states Tyldesley on the rare quality of Europe's elite competition. 'I listened to people with hundreds more England caps than me saying it was bad defending, but I watched the whole game back the next day and it wasn't.

'I'm sorry but it was wonderful attacking and a show of intent by two coaches who trusted defenders to defend one-on-one and attackers to score more than the opposition. Rob Green was my co-commentator and at the end we just put our microphones down and looked at each other and stated, "Wow.".

Recent findings suggest that 'I've not forgotten muddy pitches and assassin centre backs. You only need to look on YouTube to see football was different, but you can't pretend it was better. I see terrible games today just as I did then, but particularly in the Champions League, I regularly stumble upon football that gets me off my seat.'.

His exit from ITV, first displaced by Sam Matterface as lead commentator in 2020 and then released entirely after Euro 2024 clearly smarted but Tyldesley is comfortable as the veteran in the fast-changing media landscape.

'Most of the principles I picked up from watching John Motson, Barry Davies and Brian Moore in their pomp are applicable to commentary in 2026,' he notes. 'There's no need to reinvent that particular wheel.

'You can offer alternatives such as fan zones and screaming watchalongs for people to view it in a different way. I make it my business to look at J_Tekkz or LDN Movements or whatever is pulling in millions on YouTube.

Tyldesley believes he has not seen a better game than the first leg of PSG's Champions League semi-final with Bayern Munich last year.

The veteran commentator believes most of the principles he learned starting out still apply, but admits to having watched popular new voices to see if anything could apply to his commentary.

Tyldesley also works as a guest lecturer and commentates for blockbuster computer games, as well as selling framed prints of his commentary charts.

'I sample a bit of Mark Goldbridge to see why he's prominent but I'm hearing nothing in those guys applicable to the way I call a football match so I carry on with the same focus I've always had on what constitutes good commentary.'.

The central principle being that the game is bigger than the individuals in it, he points out, with viewers tuning in for the football not the commentator.

'The biggest challenge for a television commentator is to find the right words at the big moments, to go beyond "amazing," "brilliant", "incredible" and try to add some editorial context,' states Tyldesley.

According to recent reports, 'Every goal is unique. The words following a goal that is going to be remembered for years should be unique and specific to that goal, but that's difficult to do. It's unscripted performance and difficult to master and capture.

It has been revealed that 'I am concentrating hardest for the 10-15 seconds after a big goal because I'm searching for words which will become a small part of people's memories. That's very different to consciously trying to provide 45-second soundbites to amplify one's own personality and standing on social media.

'There's a danger of media leaning that way as it develops such an emphasis on the bitesize.'.

Among other things, Tyldesley is a guest lecturer for media students at the University of Salford, still doing commentaries for blockbuster computer games and selling framed prints of his commentary charts, something that started as 'a silly idea in lockdown'.

His wife Susan bought a dozen frames to see how it went. Originally, he offered three Champions League finals won by English clubs in 1999, 2005 and 2012. He sent one each to Gary Neville who played for Manchester United in 1999 and Jamie Carragher who played for Liverpool in 2005. They both posted images online and demand skyrocketed.

'Two good friends,' smiles Tyldesley. 'I probably got about half a million pounds of free advertising out of them.' Sales have soared beyond 50,000. There's a Celtic chart on the gym in Rod Stewart's house. Ant and Dec have bought signed Newcastle charts.

His own venture into podcasting was short-lived and he politely declines between five and ten invitations each week to appear on others.

'I've tried to step back from that kind of thing,' says Tyldesley. 'So much content I hear on football is empty, verbose and repetitive. Really, there are only so many things you can say about Alexander Isak having his shirt pulled in mid-air and Gary Neville probably said most of them in the 30 seconds following the incident.

Tyldesley has no plans to retire and Paramount, the owners of his employers CBS - and soon to be the owners of TNT Sports - will have the UK rights for the Champions League.

Sales of his framed commentary charts, something that started during lockdown, have soared beyond 50,000.

'There are so many brutally judgmental loud voices in and around football attracting attention that I want to be as far away from as possible, so that's what I do. Unless I sense an opportunity to talk about communication and broadcasting rather than whether club A, B or C should replace their manager. That's not for me Clive.'.

So, there's a little less Tyldesley out there than there was. He was content to stay at home and watch the World Cup from his sofa this summer for the first time since 1990.

But there are no intends to retire. And who knows what might change next season when Paramount, the owners of CBS – and soon to be the owners of current rights holders TNT Sports – have the UK rights for the Champions League.

There might be a familiar voice beamed into our living rooms once again.

When I saw the Dear England play, I was the only person in the theatre who didn't enjoy it, and that was because I hated the portrayal of Harry Kane.

He was written as an uneducated numbskull. Written to laugh at and the theatre laughed at him. He was stupid and gullible, another thick footballer.

And anyone who has spent time with footballers will know they might lack for an Eton College education but are streetwise and invariably smart with a razor sharp sense of humour.

In a recent development, kane is a leader of those men. There's not a single thing about the person Kane has made himself to laugh or sneer at and I wanted to stand up in the theatre that afternoon and shout at everyone.

Oddly, I was introduced to the playwright James Graham at a function a few weeks later and he kind of pushed me for my opinion of Dear England.

I tried to be diplomatic, but I felt so strongly I ended up scolding him for writing a character called Harry Kane who was nothing like Harry Kane.

It has been revealed that so, that was the end of a beautiful friendship before it began. And I'm so thrilled now there's a better appreciation of the person Harry is.

In a recent development, while a lot of soundbars are expensive (overpriced, if you ask me), the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is an instant TV speaker upgrade for just $74. I tested this soundbar two days ago and it genuinely blew me away — I couldn't believe how cheap it was. If you want to improve your home theater setup, this is the cheapest way to do it.

FKA FIFA, EA's soccer simulation game FC 27 is 57% off on the PS5 and 53% off on the Nintendo Switch 2. Yes, just two months after release. At just $27/$29 right now, this is one of the best gaming deals I've seen this Black Friday so far.

I've reviewed over 50 coffee makers — and the Casabrews 3700 Essential is the best bang-for-buck option out there. At $93, it's incomprehensibly cheap. Although it looks pretty plasticky, you're not going to get a better machine for less money — trust me, I've been there, done that.

The Casabrews 3700 Essential is my go-to recommendation for wannabe home baristas on a seriously low budget.

I remember the days when tablets were actually, genuinely cheap, and while that feels a long time ago now, the Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE is at least trying to bring it back.

According to recent reports, right now, the Galaxy Tab S10 FE is $349 down from $549, which makes it one of the best-value tablets out there. You get IP68 water resistance (so it'll survive dunks in the bathtub), Handwriting Assist (I need that!), and the best part? You get a free pen included. No need to buy a stylus (coughApplecough).

You have to be super quick with this one — Amazon has discounted its Echo Spot smart speakers to just $84. That's a huge 61% off! This is a pack of two, so you'd get one for your nightstand and one for your home office (or kitchen, or bathroom, or living room...).

Sources indicate that however, this discount won't last forever. 8% have already been claimed, or you've got 22 hours left — whichever empties first.

The Amazon Ember 4-Series is one of Amazon's entry-level own-brand TVs — and all sizes are just $0.04 off their lowest-ever prices. Yes, seriously — these TVs are $199.99, whereas the lowest-ever price is $199.95. You know what? I'd classify this as the lowest-ever price.

I tested the Ember 4-Series earlier this year, and while it's not technically the brightest 4K TV on the market, it's fantastic if you're on a budget. You can access Alexa+, which means you can ask the TV for recommendations if you're stuck on what to watch.

If I were buying a TV on a budget, the Ember 4-Series would be up there.

In a recent development, there's no better brand for ANC — Bose is the King. Dr. Bose literally invented ANC. Other audio brands try, and they do succeed, but Bose's ANC is just something else. I've tested almost everything the American audio giant has to offer: the QuietComfort Earbuds, QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds, QuietComfort Headphones (these ones), the QuietComfort Headphones Ultra 2nd Gen... and seriously, no other ANC comes close.

Sources indicate that if you're a frequent traveller, I wholeheartedly recommend Bose headphones. Right now, the Bose QuietComfort Headphones are $169 down from $359. Sure, they're technically "last year's" model now that the 2nd Gen are here, but I don't think they're by any means outdated. My dad rocks his pair (that he bought because I told him to!).

According to recent reports, as a voracious reader, I have an overflowing bookshelf, a Kobo, and a Kindle. I just can't get enough of the written word. If I don't read everyday, my brain starts doing weird things.

I tested the Kindle Colorsoft earlier this year and loved it. Kindle Unlimited is a pretty sweet deal: read as many books as you want for $11 a month. That's the biggest downside of a Kobo — you don't get to capitalise on Amazon's extremely thorough catalogue. (Although I love my Kobo, too!).

Our No.1 best Garmin smartwatch is the Forerunner 570, presently $100 off at Amazon. While I'd like to see a bigger discount than 18%, the Forerunner 570's lowest-ever price is $448 — so we're just $1 off.

Sources indicate that judging by historical sales events, the Forerunner 570 won't get any cheaper than $448. If you've been looking at investing in a Garmin watch, now might be the best time.

The Ninja BlendSense series of blenders is almost incomprehensibly powerful. It can make nut butter in minutes with very little manual interference, and it's also the best kitchen assistant. I make kimchi semi-regularly, so I chuck all my ingredients — whole onions, garlic, carrots, and radish — into the blender, and five seconds later I've got perfectly minced veg.

And you know when you can never quite clean a blender because the blades are in the way? Not a problem on the BlendSense. The blades are 100% removable, so you can get every scrap of food out. I've got the Detect Power Pro, but this model has the same tech but with more blades and blending cups.

While $179 isn't quite its lowest price ever of $169, it's only $10 off.

The world’s smallest smart ring just got its first major discount. The Oura Ring 5 came out earlier this year — and we gave it a near-perfect 4.5-star rating in our review. As I write this, it’s still available in all sizes (from 6 to 13), and you can also get a sizing kit if you’re not sure which one to buy.

Industry observers note that tom's Guide Fitness Managing Editor Jane McGuire noted she "struggled to find a flaw or missing feature" on the Oura Ring 5 after testing for a month. "By chopping 40% of the bulk while actually extending the battery life, Oura hasn't followed the tech trend of making slight tweaks to launch a new product — it has completely rewritten the blueprint for what invisible tech can do.".

Of course, there's no discount on the $5.99 monthly subscription.

I'm Erin, and I'm a Senior Reviews Writer. That means I've tested tons of products, from your flagship Apple AirPods Max 2 to coffee machines by brands no one's heard of.

That also means I know what a good deal is — after testing over 200 products, I have enough first-hand experience with garbage to help you avoid said garbage.

So sit back, relax, and let me do all the hard work!

Why Black Friday and Cyber Monday Are Bad Days to Impulse Buy Electronics

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Follow our live blog to stay up-to-date on the best sales we find.

Browse our editors’ picks for a curated list of our favorite sales on laptops, fitness tech, appliances, and more.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a big "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be noted for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Sources indicate that because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before newly introduced models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

It has been revealed that price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In a recent development, in the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The concern isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

Industry observers note that the key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

It has been revealed that to avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

According to recent reports, if you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

Industry observers note that yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Recent findings suggest that yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Sources indicate that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

According to recent reports, black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.
